Saatva makes more than a dozen luxury mattresses, including the Saatva Rx mattress for chronic back pain and a memory foam hybrid mattress that layers cooling foam over coils. The four below made our list of the best Black Friday deals, and they vary by what’s inside.

"[My husband and I] both sleep warm and appreciate the vented airflow channels, which allow for circulation," she says in her review. She also found her lower back pain went away after the switch. In most shared beds, somebody is compromising on firmness. The comfort layers on top flip, too: latex side up for more bounce, foam side up for more give. Saatva recommends the softer settings for side sleepers and the firmer end for stomach sleepers. Pair a split king with Saatva's split adjustable base and each side can change its position as well as its firmness.

Saatva's first all-foam mattress skips springs entirely, so it molds to your body and lets you sink in slightly. It pairs two layers of cooling gel-infused memory foam with a high-density foam base that keeps movement from traveling across the bed. Contributor Bailey Berg, who considers anything north of 70 degrees hot, chose it for that gel foam and went with the firm option over relaxed firm to sleep cooler still. The dense base was the bigger surprise. "Both my partner and I are light sleepers: If one of us rolls over, the other one generally wakes up too," she says in her review. "After the first couple nights, I realized I hadn't been woken up by his movements (or by our dogs jumping on and off the bed) at all." Four years in, she reports no sag in the center, no dips where they sleep, and an organic cotton cover that has softened without pilling. If running warm is your main complaint, Saatva's newer all-foam model, the Contour5, adds a heat-dispersing CoolVent cooling system and a phase-change lumbar layer.

A shredded latex core cushions the head, neck, and shoulders in any position, and contributor Sydney Gore found that it eased her back issues. "You won't have to buy new pillows for years afterwards," she says in her best pillows review. Buy two and save up to $60. Send the second one to the guest room.

Saatva's organic sateen set is 300-thread-count long-staple cotton, GOTS certified organic, woven one yarn over and three under, which is what gives sateen its silky hand and soft sheen. The fitted sheet's deep pockets fit mattresses up to 16 inches tall, so it works on the taller Classic, and the set comes in white only. If you'd rather sleep on something crisp, contributor Katarina Kovac swears by the brand's percale for how airy the weave feels.

If a new mattress isn't in the cards this year, a topper is the next best fix. This one is three inches of organic natural latex quilted in organic wool under an organic cotton cover, and Saatva describes the feel as plush with medium firmness. It fits any mattress, Saatva's or otherwise, and the brand pitches it for softening a new bed during the break-in period or buying an old one a few more years.

For anyone who loves memory foam but not how warm it can run, this three-inch topper infuses the foam with graphite, which Saatva says draws body heat away, and wraps it in a breathable organic cotton blend cover. It's medium-firm with the contouring hug memory foam is known for, and Saatva recommends it for every sleep position, side sleepers especially. The foams are CertiPUR-US certified.

The softest of Saatva's toppers adds about two inches of down-alternative fill split into two chambers: a finer fiber on top for loft and a sturdier one underneath so you don't bottom out. Baffle-box stitching keeps the fill from drifting into one corner, a fitted skirt keeps the topper from sliding, and the 300-thread-count sateen cover is breathable. It's hypoallergenic and OEKO-TEX certified, which makes it an easy upgrade for a guest bed when you don't know who'll be sleeping in it.

The main draw is a one-touch zero-gravity button, which raises your feet to heart level and lifts your head and knees slightly for balanced support. There's also a head, full-body, and foot massage with three intensity levels, an anti-snore preset that tilts the head up seven degrees, under-bed LED lighting, and USB ports for your phone. Buy it with a mattress for $100 off. It works with every Saatva mattress except the 14.5-inch Classic and the youth and crib models, and adjustable bases can't be returned, so measure before you order.

With rounded edges and fluted drawers in natural oak, the Arden would look as at home in a beach house as in a city bedroom. Buy two and Saatva takes $200 off, which is how most people buy nightstands anyway.

This low-profile platform frame stands on slim legs that lift it off the floor, with a kiln-dried hardwood frame and plywood slats that let you skip the box spring. The back of the headboard is fully upholstered (it's shown in graphite velvet), so the bed can sit in the middle of a room without an unfinished side facing the door. It also works with Saatva's adjustable bases, and buying it with a mattress takes $100 off.

#4785. Franklin Templeton makes room for HYPE in crypto index ETF

The addition comes as US spot investment products tracking Hyperliquid’s native token reach $266.5 million in assets under management.

Asset manager Franklin Templeton plans to add the Hyperliquid (HYPE) token to its crypto index exchange-traded fund (ETF), according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Nov. 25.

The token will be added to the Franklin Crypto Index ETF on Dec. 1, following HYPE’s inclusion in the fund’s benchmark. The fund, which trades under the ticker EZPZ, currently holds Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH), XRP, Solana (SOL), Dogecoin (DOGE), Cardano (ADA) and Lumen (XLM).

Hyperliquid, a layer-1 blockchain that hosts a decentralized exchange specializing in perpetual futures trading, has seen its total value locked rise to $7.3 billion from $4.13 billion in early January. The protocol generated $80.3 million in revenue over the past 30 days, according to DefiLlama.

Its native token, HYPE, is used to pay network fees and can be staked to earn rewards. The protocol also uses a portion of its trading fee revenue to buy back HYPE on the open market, linking trading activity on the platform to demand for the token.

Related: HYPE teases all-time high as NYSE owner ICE eyes US Hyperliquid perps

Franklin Templeton’s move comes as more investment products offer exposure to HYPE.

Three US spot exchange-traded products (ETPs) tracking HYPE have launched since May, with offerings from asset managers 21Shares, Bitwise and Grayscale. They collectively held approximately $266.5 million in assets under management as of Nov. 27, according to Coinperps data.

These products allow US investors to gain exposure to the Hyperliquid ecosystem through traditional financial rails without having to directly hold the token.

The exchange ranks among the largest venues for decentralized perpetual futures trading, although its official interface remains restricted to US users. Perpetual futures are derivative contracts that allow traders to speculate on an asset’s price movements without a fixed expiration date.

President Donald Trump said in August that Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chair Michael Selig was working to bring Hyperliquid into the US in compliance with regulations.

Related: Hong Kong adds Hyperliquid to list of ‘suspicious’ crypto platforms

#4781. Samsung Frame Pro TV Review, Tested by AD (2026)

A staple in most modern homes, televisions often war against the ongoing aesthetics of a space in their off-time. Masquerading as artwork, the Samsung Frame TV offers an alternative in the world of home entertainment that amplifies interior design instead of taking away from it.

Eagle eyes will have spotted the Frame across many of our home tours—including some celebrity abodes, like the living room of Jesse Tyler Ferguson’s New York pied-a-terre. With their art-forward ideology, it’s clear to see why the Frame line is favored by designers. After all, a big black screen is not really enhancing the visual impact of a living room.

As a design devotee and AD’s resident television and film-obsessive, I tried out the Frame Pro to see if it really measured up. Boasting the same matte finish display as the original model but with brighter picture quality, fully wireless outputs, and a bevy of technical upgrades, the Frame Pro has features to offer for tech purists and design-heads alike.

How much does it cost? Are there payment plans available?

The Frame Pro starts at $2,200—though is already marked down for Black Friday, and may drop further in price closer to the shopping holiday. Payment plans are available through Affirm, with options up to four installments, the lowest being $400 every two weeks.

The Frame Pro comes in three sizes, starting at 65 inches and going up in ten inch intervals to 85 inches. I opted for the smallest size to best fit my available wall space, and chose a white bezel border (brown and teak are the other colorways) to coordinate with the frames on the wall art in my living room.

A service coordinated the delivery window with me over email and helped to set up the television once they arrived to make sure it was functioning properly. Despite what the name would have you believe, the Frame Pro does, in fact, have attachable legs. The delivery service did not include mounting, so the team merely helped lift the Frame Pro onto my TV stand and set it up in a freestanding format.

What was the installation process like? How long did it take, and how many people?

The Frame Pro has a very slim mounting system consisting of two brackets. The installation kit comes with a paper template with the layout of the brackets printed on it. The process was fairly straightforward, though I wish the step-by-step manual had more text included rather than just showing images of the process.

Although the brackets have several slots to accommodate differing stud widths, we ran into an issue where the distance between the studs in our building didn’t quite align with the bracket slots to center it on the wall while also keeping the TV secure in the studs. In the end, we ended up hanging the TV ever so slightly off-center in order to keep the screws aligned with the studs. For peace of mind, we added drywall anchors and screws to the center-most slots of the bracket for some additional support to help distribute the weight a bit more.

Hanging the TV from the bracket was simple, and because the screw-in panels on the back are magnetized, it made it feel more secure when we slotted it into place. At just under 50 pounds, the TV wasn’t all that heavy, though because of the larger size, we did need two people (and another to guide the way) to lift it in place. The bezel is also magnetized, so the four pieces simply snap onto the exterior of the TV once you have it hung up.

Overall, the mounting process took us about two hours to complete but I think it could likely be decreased down to one hour (and possibly even less) had it not been for our particular issues with the stud distances that needed a lot of remeasuring and even a last-minute trip to the hardware store for a stud finder.

As the Frame’s main draw, I was most eager to see art mode in action. The artwork is selected either through Samsung’s Art Store (which requires a $4.99 per month subscription) or through personally uploaded photos to the SmartThings companion app. To really be convincing as artwork, the photos need to be high quality—you wouldn’t notice any blurriness when seeing the Mona Lisa at the Louvre, would you? For older artworks, I was able to find plenty of high resolution files available for free through museum or crowdsourced websites. Once you make sure its resolution matches the 4K sizing of the Frame (3,840 x 2,160 pixels), you simply upload the image and select if you want a matboard added to the border. If you upload a smaller size image, you can expect to see some amount of graininess once it loads on the screen. I chose a selection of paintings by Vincent Van Gogh, Georgia O’Keefe, and Claude Monet, among other artists with the rotating gallery feature. While essentially all the artwork I tested out looked beautiful on the screen, the paintings with thicker brushstrokes made me want to reach out and touch it to see if it was real.

I found that the art mode is most convincing when you’re in a well-lit room. Even though the TV brightness does adjust automatically—and has motion sensors so it only turns on when someone enters a room if you want to leave it on all day—the fact that it’s a screen becomes more obvious in low-light environments. Even at its lowest brightness setting, when in art mode in a dark room, the screen slightly illuminates the space, no longer tricking your eyes that it’s artwork.

In terms of the viewing experience, the Frame Pro certainly leveled up my weekly binge watches. The image is incredibly crisp, and when rewatching shows I’d seen before (I’m a creature of habit, what can I say), I noticed the colors were markedly more vivid than on my previous TV. The Neo QLED panel, a.k.a. mini LEDs, makes a big difference in the contrast of colors on the TV, and it’s all the more enjoyable to see ingenious set designs from my favorite shows and movies.

One of the big differences between the Frame Pro and previous models is the Wireless One Connect box. Where the regular Frame model has a slim transparent cord connected to the box that contains HDMI and other outputs, the Frame Pro is fully wireless, meaning the only cable coming out of the TV is the power cord. I have fairly speedy and reliable internet so there haven’t been any issues with connection being wireless. Plus, I love the clean look the lack of cords provides. The only time I noticed lag was when I tried using Chromecast from my phone to try and stream content. It took longer to load and had some clarity issues in the picture. That’s not true for everything I cast, as a movie I mirrored through AirPlay loaded easily, so I think it might have been due to an incompatibility with Google’s casting software or the phone it was being routed through.

I’ve had the Frame Pro for over a year now and haven’t noticed any difference in visual quality or functionality when watching different shows or movies. Style-wise, I’ve loved decorating around the Frame as the seasons change. The minimalist white base doesn’t detract from surrounding decor, like pumpkins during Halloween and garland and ornaments around Christmas. I’ve subbed in a few different pieces of artwork in the art library, particularly during hosting season when I want to curate a cozier vibe with an autumnal artwork or yule log video. The automatic software updates keep the TV functioning at a high level, even as streaming apps regularly change.

It’s safe to say that I’m keeping this TV for as long as possible. Even as someone who loves to watch shows and movies, I don’t want the entire design of my living room to revolve around a television. The slim design of the Frame really shifts the focus to the other furniture and decor in the space, and makes my space feel more centered around the memories made inside it.

#4780. Binance plans Asia hub in Bhutan, receives preliminary approval

The agreement is a milestone in Binance’s effort to expand its presence in Bhutan since launching a national crypto-powered tourism payment system in 2025.

Binance has received in-principle approval from the Gelephu Central Bank (GCB) to establish regulated digital-asset operations in Bhutan’s Gelephu Mindfulness City (GMC).

Binance signed an agreement on a broad partnership and plans for Gelephu Mindfulness City to become an Asia hub for Binance users, according to a Saturday news release.

Jigdrel Singay, GMC board director, said “Binance choosing Gelephu Mindfulness City as a base for its Asia operations is an important milestone for what we are building in Bhutan. Our ambition is not simply to attract global companies to establish an entity here. We want them to build real operations, create meaningful jobs, develop talent and transfer capabilities that remain in the country over the long term.

“The in-principle approval is an important first step, and we look forward to working closely with Binance and GCB as Binance completes the remaining regulatory requirements and builds its presence in GMC,” Singay added.

The agreement is a milestone in Binance’s effort to expand its presence in Bhutan since launching a national crypto-powered tourism payment system in 2025. The company plans to continue building out the local digital-asset ecosystem, according to the release.

Related: Nansen to set up Bhutan entity in Gelephu Mindfulness City

Cointelegraph had reported in May that Gelephu Mindfulness City was offering an accelerated licensing pathway for crypto and fintech companies already regulated in hubs like Singapore, Hong Kong and Abu Dhabi, as the Himalayan territory pushes to position itself as a new South Asian financial center.

The move reflects growing competition among emerging jurisdictions seeking to attract crypto firms with streamlined regulation, banking access and tax incentives, as global regulators tighten oversight and warn against regulatory arbitrage.

Singay stressed in May that the system is not a passport for offshore licenses and that firms must be authorized under GMC’s rules.

The IPA is not a full license, the release confirmed, as Binance must satisfy the conditions specified by GCB and complete the remaining regulatory requirements.

Binance will now work with Bhutan’s central bank to complete the regulatory requirements for a full license.

#4777. The Best Treadmills for Your Home Gym, Tested by Fitness Editors

We've logged hundreds of miles on each during our testing.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE TREADMILL IS one of the most basic and essential tools of a good cardio routine. Being able to move your own bodyweight from Point A to Point B is pretty critical in daily life as well, making walking and running the most functional exercises around. But what if you don’t want to drop money on a monthly membership for a gym 30 minutes away, just to use their banged up and outdated machines?

A great treadmill can be a powerful ally in helping you keep up your fitness and not miss a step in your training. If you’re planning to purchase a treadmill for your home, you should know that it’s no small investment. But with the high level of competition in the marketplace and more stock available than years past, now is a perfect time to take the leap. Whether you want to train for a marathon, build endurance with intense weighted-vest walks on an incline, get the blood pumping between errands, or all of the above, there’s a machine out there for you.

Out of all the treadmills we've tested, we believe that the NordicTrack T10 Treadmill is a reliable choice for most people to use at home, given its durability, performance, and overall value. Its design is simplistic and user-friendly, with a modest touchscreen that offers preset programs and entertainment. For those seeking an added layer of motivation, an optional subscription for on-board workout content is available as an add-on.

We’ve put together a guide to the best treadmills, tested by our editors (who happen to be certified trainers), that will help you torch calories and chase your fitness goals at home.

The NordicTrack 1750 has been a long-standing favorite among MH fitness editors and hardcore indoor runners for years, and with good reason: It’s an all-around winner. The 16-inch touchscreen is responsive and compatible with iFIT programming, and the newest edition features both incline and decline.

The 1750 is one of the most stable treadmills we've ever been on, likely thanks to its durable build and powerful 3.5 CHP motor. The frame doesn't buckle or shake at all when you are putting in those hard miles. Other things to love include the 22-inch by 60-inch deck, which is outfitted with generous cushioning, and the new lower step up height, making it more accessible for all runners. We enjoy how cushioned the landing feels with our feet being cradled with each stride. This treadmill offers speeds of up to 12 MPH and an incline of up to 12%, meaning it can keep up with most running goals. This treadmill is much quieter than other models that we've run on in the past. Whether we're doing incline jogs or finishing with sprints, it can handle it all.NordicTrack's iFit content bring a lot of value, and the addition of this programming to your use of the treadmill can really elevate it. Most of the time, when you are getting technology with next-level technology, you have to be delicate with the machinery. But the 1750 is built like a tank, and in our testing was able to withstand our most punishing sprint sessions.

The only two things we'd change on this machine would be to extend the 10-year frame warranty (we'd love for it to be 15) and make the machine easier to move. Otherwise, this treadmill is a sure-fire winner.

Need an affordable treadmill that can satisfy tight space constraints? The XTERRA TR75 Sport Series is the best machine we've tested that fits the bill, all for just around $1,000. Even less if it happens to be on sale. Despite its low cost, it delivers a level of reliability uncommon among similarly priced treadmills.

During our testing, we were surprised at how quiet the belt and motor performed when maxing out at 12 MPH and 12% incline, though the machine did whine a bit as it adjusted to our desired incline. It is extremely lightweight and compact, yet the steel frame feels solid, and the foldable design adds to its practicality for home use.

The 'Lift Assist and Slow Deploy' mechanism exceeded our initial expectations, making it ridiculously effortless to fold and unfold the machine. It also has wheels. This is a machine that won't cause stress, a ton of logistical planning, and doesn't require multiple hands if you ever need to relocate from one room to another. One person could manage it alone, no problem.

Unlike treadmills with interactive touchscreens, this model is a little less tech-savvy, with a 6.5-inch LCD display. While it does offer some built-in training programs and Bluetooth connectivity for third-party apps that we found intuitive to work with, it lacks the smart features and finishes of higher-end models. But after all, at this price point, it isn't pretending to compete in that class of cardio machines.

Above all, this treadmill boasts a great value. In our experience testing budget-to-premium treadmills, a lower price tag often comes at the expense of build quality, weight capacity, and deck size. The TR75 defies this trend. Its 350-pound user weight capacity surpasses the industry standard, the 60-inch by 20-inch deck offers ample space suitable for taller individuals, and it provides enough power to meet most training needs.

The NordicTrack T10 treadmill takes the lead in the tech-forward, reasonably-priced T series. For those who would like a slightly smaller, less expensive version with all the same high-tech features that the Commercial 1750 comes with, this is the treadmill for you.

When using this machine, we were impressed by the solid build and easy-to-use controls. The touchscreen display is flanked by quick key buttons to adjust speed and incline to your liking in one touch, instead of repeatedly pressing a button while trying to speed up or slow down.

Equipped with a 3.0 continuous HP motor, this treadmill offers the industry standard speed of up to 12 MPH and an incline of up to 12%. Much like other models in the NordicTrack system, this piece of equipment handles impact well. Like the more expensive options from the brand, you feel cushioned and cradled with each stride.

One of the great features of this model is its storability, which comes without sacrificing a whole lot of features. They have even been able to find a way to keep the belt size as 60 inches, the same as the more premium NordicTrack options.

This model also features a 10-inch HD touchscreen display that provides on-demand instructor-led classes and programs to guide your runs at any time. The touchscreen display is smaller than other high-tech models, but it gets the job done.

Part of the new Strive Series from REP Fitness, this curved treadmill takes the category and puts all other designs on notice. Offering a more ergonomic running experience, the curved treadmill burns more calories while reducing impact on your joints.

When we say durable, we mean it. This manual machine can support users up to 400 pounds, and we never had to worry about its tech features glitching or lagging—because there aren't any. Since this machine relies entirely on the user's power (not an external power source), I could maneuver it on its wheels from the garage to the driveway for a breath of fresh air whenever I felt like it.

It's worth noting, however, that moving this treadmill up or down a flight of stairs without multiple pairs of hands isn't advisable. It weighs 418 pounds and lacks any folding or compacting capabilities, so it requires a team to unbox and set up, plus a permanent space to house this beast.

The Peloton Tread takes on the familiar feeling of a live studio experience, initially popularized by the Peloton Bike and compatible app. We recommend the Peloton Tread for those who like a group class environment from the comfort of their own home.

We found that the massive 24" HD touchscreen simulates the camaraderie of running in a race better than any other machine, fostering a competitive-yet-supportive class environment. And now with the new Cross-Training version, the screen swivels fully, allowing you to use it for the strength classes available on demand as well.

This experience helps to increase how much people actually use their treadmills. Translation: Sure, this baby is expensive, but it’s worth the money. It’s an experience unlike any other that pretty much everyone has tried to copy.

The 59-inch by 20-inch deck is large enough for almost any-sized runner, and the 300-pound user weight capacity hits the industry standards we’d expect to see. The newly-added Tread lock makes this machine (now) safe to have around kids and pets who may be tempted to climb and play on it.

Despite the lofty price point, be sure to avoid the temptation of buying a discounted used machine and get yours new. In the past, it's unfortunately been prone to maintenance-related issues, so you’ll want a warranty in case anything happens to yours.

If you're a serious runner looking for a treadmill that can handle serious training, this is it. It's an absolute powerhouse. The frame itself is exceptionally sturdy, and we didn't detect any shaking even when running at a push pace (it goes up to 12 MPH). We also find this treadmill especially great for interval training and hills when we want to switch things up, given its broad decline/incline range.

For bigger users looking to boost their cardio, this treadmill has a 350-pound user weight capacity, surpassing the industry standard by 100 pounds. On top of that, it was built to take a beating, so it can handle any exercise you throw at it, no matter the intensity.

The downside of this machine's durability and solid feel is that it's (unsurprisingly) quite heavy. Weighing in at 323 pounds, moving it requires at least two pairs of hands (and some gusto), even with the included transport wheels. For this reason, you'll need to designate a dedicated spot for this treadmill, as it's not as compact as some other models when folded. That spot will need to be quite spacious, as this treadmill is wider (and a tad longer) than most comparable home machines.

On the plus side, the extra-large 22-inch by 60-inch deck more than compensates for its substantial footprint. We can open up our stride on this machine and never feel crammed or cut short. Bowflex's commitment to quality is evident in its warranty, which offers 15-year frame coverage (on par with the industry standard).

It's also remarkably easy to set up, thanks to straightforward assembly instructions that take less than an hour to complete.

When you are building a home gym, space is a precious resource, and treadmills can take up a significant amount. Be sure to check the dimensions of any treadmill you're considering. Add at least 1-2 feet in every direction, and 3 feet or more behind the treadmill (the area you step onto the machine from) for maximum safety.

One thing buyers also tend to overlook is the height. You’ll want at least 15” inches above your own height when standing on the treadmill. So, if you’re 5’10” (70 inches), make sure your ceiling height is enough to accommodate 85 inches, plus the height of the treadmill belt. This is especially important if you’re planning to use your treadmill for running.

Lastly, consider how much storage space you'll need if you aren’t planning to leave the treadmill out when you aren’t working out. Great folding treadmill options and models can be moved or positioned easily, helping you make the most of the space between runs.

Looking for a treadmill suitable for running? Or maybe you just want a reliable machine to walk on while you watch TV. Whatever you’re looking for, make sure the deck size suits your activity preferences (and your height). The industry standard for a walking treadmill deck is 55 inches by 20 inches, and at least 60 inches by 20 inches for running. You may be able to get away with running or walking on shorter decks, but that means altering your stride length, so you’ll have to think about every step you take.

This might seem obvious, but double-check that all four corners of the treadmill are firmly on the floor after setup. Many home floors aren’t 100% level (you'd be surprised). Make sure your treadmill is well-planted to minimize the risk of slippage, shifting, or tilting.

Treadmills can—and often do—make a lot of noise, especially for your downstairs neighbors (if you live in an apartment) or housemates (if you live in a multi-story house). If you think this might be an issue, consider a treadmill mat to help minimize the noise. These simple, usually affordable mats can help deaden sound and vibration on the floor beneath a treadmill. However, they won't quiet the belt itself, and we’ve suggested models that won’t screech above your gym playlist.

Treadmills, especially large and commercial models, can draw significant power. If your home’s electrical setup allows, dedicate one circuit to just your treadmill. This helps ensure other power-hungry devices on that same circuit don’t blow a fuse.

Nobody wants to spend money on a treadmill that won’t keep up with their workouts. Decide what speeds and inclines you'll need for your training goals. Treadmills vary in capacity for these features, and while 12 mph might be enough for some, it may not be enough for sprinters.

The same goes with inclines. Most brands are transparent about the motor’s horsepower, but some don’t disclose it on the treadmill’s spec sheet. For reference, you should look for at least a 3.0 CHP motor if you plan to run or sprint regularly.

The industry standard for a treadmill frame warranty is 15 years to life. This is the standard for mid- to high-dollar treadmills, but if you’re buying some random machine off of Amazon for $200, don’t expect this type of guarantee. We also recommend registering your machine on the brand’s website right after purchase to make sure you can cash in on the warranty if you ever need to.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to test all kinds of home gym equipment, including treadmills. Our team at MH includes former athletes, marathoners, and certified trainers, and we conferenced on the best treadmills for all types of use. Over the years, our dedicated editors have rigorously tested treadmills from reliable, top-rated brands, evaluating performance, user experience, size, durability, and overall value.

To ensure a comprehensive assessment of each product, the team put each treadmill through the wringer with a variety of workouts, including sprints, long-distance runs, and tempo runs. We did this at home, in the Men's Health gym, and at various training facilities around the world. Together, we've logged hundreds of miles on each treadmill, giving us valuable insights into how it stacks up against other options on the market.

We also made sure we're up to date on industry standards (motor horsepower, warranty, incline/decline options, and speed) and the components that make an excellent treadmill versus a ‘meh’ one. From that research and testing, we deduced the front runners and best treadmills in the pack.

Maybe. It all depends on your personal fitness level and goals. Curved treadmills are non-motorized. They rely instead on you walking or running, and the belt being pushed backward manually with every foot strike on the sloped surface. While this might not seem as "fancy" or high-tech as a powered treadmill, this design has its benefits.

"Curved treadmills tend to recruit more muscles due to the shape of the belt and the act of propelling against it," says Eric Sung, C.S.C.S., a member of the Men's Health Strength in Diversity initiative and trainer at Performance Lab in New York City. "It also eases the strain of your joints because of the curvature and is often better for users with varied joint pain."

By some reports, exercising on a curved treadmill burns 30% more calories over a traditional powered treadmill.

"One drawback of a curved treadmill is that it is difficult to achieve higher speeds (sprints) with proper technique. This can impact front side mechanics with one's stride through by 'reaching'," explains Sung. Another thing to consider: Because curved treads are motorless, they also don't allow for incline or decline capabilities.

Yes, although not critically, according to David Siik, founder of Precision Run by Equinox.

"To create a sense of security, people tend to run far too close to the front of the treadmill," he explains. This can lead to a compressed posture, restricting the range of motion in your arms. Siik recommends maintaining at least one foot of distance between your belly and the treadmill monitor.

Treadmills may require slightly less engagement of our hamstrings compared to outdoor running, though the difference isn't substantial, Siik tells us.

"Another important point we emphasize with our runners and walkers is the importance of avoiding the habit of constantly staring at your phone while using the treadmill." Over time, this posture can strain your neck.

Jonathan Cane, an exercise physiologist, running coach, and founder of City Coach Multisport in New York City, highlights several benefits of running on a treadmill. He mentions that treadmills allow for the simulation of terrain, making them valuable for training when natural hills or elevation changes aren't readily available. This feature is particularly useful for preparing for hilly races.

"Walking up a grade can have comparable cardiovascular benefit to running flat, yet doesn't have the associated orthopedic stress, so it can be a great way to get a workout without all the pounding you might have with running," he explains.

Siik explains that the benefits of running and walking on an incline boil down to the increased energy spend (remaining calories burned) caused by the increased power needed to climb vertically.

"Variation is key to experience the full benefits of incline. Steep inclines have wonderful energy burning benefits but also can destabilize the knees over time if done frequently," he explains. "This is why the treadmill is beautiful for incline training; it allows you to play with such a spectrum of programming."

Treadmills also offer the advantage of being weather-independent, with modern models featuring softer surfaces that are gentler on the body compared to running on hard asphalt or concrete. (Remember: Running outside exposes you to the elements, which can have additional mental and physical benefits, so do it when possible.)

#4775. ASEAN+3 agrees on initiative to explore crypto payments cooperation

A working group will examine enhancing connectivity between domestic digital payment networks and bringing their regulations into more alignment.

China, Japan, South Korea and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) will establish a working group aimed at enhancing connectivity between domestic digital payment networks and bringing their regulatory approaches into more alignment.

The ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) will oversee the program, according to a statement issued by Japan’s Ministry of Finance.

The agreement was reached at the ASEAN+3 Finance and Central Bank Deputies’ Meeting in Kyoto that concluded on Thursday.

Cointelegraph, meanwhile, reported on Friday that Binance co-founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao favors crypto license passporting across ASEAN, arguing that firms regulated in one market should be able to enter others through a simplified approval process rather than applying from scratch.

While moving toward greater cooperation, member states still regulate digital assets separately, creating multiple approval processes for companies seeking a regional presence.

Speaking at a fireside chat at the ASEAN Tech Summit Manila 2026, Zhao backed an idea raised by FinTech Alliance PH founding chair Lito Villanueva for regulatory passporting or license portability.

A regional licensing framework could reduce compliance costs, encourage competition and make it easier for crypto and stablecoin services to operate across ASEAN’s fragmented regulatory markets.

#4770. The Hybrid Training Formula to Run Fast and Lift Heavy

Get the split right, then pick shoes that match the work.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

RUNNING SOMETIMES GETS a bad rap in the weight room, as if a few laps around the block will somehow undo all those hard-earned gains. Turns out, the two activities aren’t the rivals they’re made out to be. Adding miles to your strength routine can build endurance to back up all that muscle. A review study found that combining aerobic exercise with resistance training produced gains in muscle size and maximal strength similar to lifting alone. The benefits work in reverse, too: Smart strength work can also help make you a more efficient runner.

The result? A body that can move serious weight, cover some ground, and handle whatever else you throw at it. Of course, getting the most out of running and lifting takes some strategy, from how you schedule your workouts to how you manage recovery. Another important factor is foot health, which can affect both your big lifts and running splits.

Here’s how to balance running and lifting in your routine, strengthen the feet that support both, and choose shoes for each workout.

YOUR TRAINING SCHEDULE should reflect your priorities. Focused on building strength? Keep your toughest gym sessions front and center and work easy-paced runs around them. Training for a race? Schedule your key runs first. “If your goal is strength, you can’t show up tired,” says Courtney Conley, DC, a chiropractic physician specializing in foot mechanics who recommends separating demanding running and lifting workouts when possible to allow for recovery. Either way, she suggests hitting the weights two to three times a week without going all-out every session.

But if you’re running and strength training, consider also building your explosive power. “You have to train the spring, train that reactive quickness,” Conley says. This is where plyometrics like jumps and hops train you to generate force quickly, absorb impact, and rebound. And, this comes in handy whether you’re sprinting, changing direction on the court, or charging uphill. It will also help your big lifts in the gym, particularly squats, deadlifts, and any type of Olympic lift because it develops things like neuromuscular coordination—allowing you to implement full-body movement patterns and stabilize heavy loads faster; and the rate of force development—how fast you can turn your strength on.

Just make sure you train this way early in your workout, not at the end. “You don’t want to do plyometric training when you’re fatigued,” Conley cautions. Doing so can compromise your form, making those explosive moves less effective and potentially increasing your risk of injury.

THE BODYPART THAT makes all of this training possible is your feet. Their small muscles help you maintain balance, support your arches, and control movement under load. During a squat, for example, those muscles help provide a stable base as you drive through your legs and hips. “Deadlifting is a foot action,” Conley explains. “You’ve got to feel your mid foot and press it into the ground to stabilize your body.”

Running demands just as much. Every stride is essentially a single-leg hop, with your feet and ankles absorbing impact, storing energy, and releasing it to propel you forward. In her practice, Conley sometimes sees clients with weak feet or Achilles issues. “When they go to hop, they sink into the ground, and there’s just no spring out of that system.” It’s one more reason those muscles below your ankles deserve just as much attention as your quads and glutes.

And while you could do specific mobility exercises for your feet, those small muscles get quite a workout when performing single-leg moves that help build strength, balance, and stability.

WHEN YOU TRADE weights for miles, what you need underfoot changes. Your plush running shoes may be great on the road, but they’re no match for the weight room. “When you’re in the gym and you want to lift heavy things, you cannot be wearing your 45 millimeter stack height cushion shoe that has a toe spring on it,” Conley says. “You can’t feel the ground.” For strength training, look for a firm, relatively flat sole that keeps you grounded when the weights get heavy.

One thing to consider is looking for a shoe that allows for balanced weight distribution across the foot. Another is a wide toe-box that allows for your toes to splay. When your big toe has the space to remain straight, it can help keep you stable. It’s this last principle behind the Altra Fit that allows your foot to function naturally: a roomy toe box that gives your toes space while keeping the midfoot secure, rather than making the whole shoe wider. “The widest part of your foot should be your toes,” Conley explains.

And it is this design that can help you choose shoes for running, strength training, or both, that allow your feet to get stronger during all these activities because they support them. “The whole reason I love Altra running shoes so much is because they respect the anatomy of the foot,” Conley says.

Altra offers different cushioning levels, stack heights, and heel-to-toe drops. “If you’re new to this conversation of foot health and strength training, you cannot go zero to 100,” Conley says. In other words, match your shoes to the workout, and if you’re switching to lower-stack or zero-drop footwear, give your feet and calves time to adapt. Here are some Altra shoes to consider:

If you are someone who goes from the weight room to a run (or vice versa), the Escalante 5 keeps things lean with a 24mm stack that has a zero-drop and wide toebox that gives you a stable platform during your heaviest lifts. And for your runs, the responsive EGO cushioning allows you to strengthen your foot with each step no matter whether you are leisurely jogging, crushing speedwork, or doing errands.

If you like to hit the trails with some weight training on the side, the Lone Peak 9 adds a little more cushioning and a grippy MaxTrac outsole for tackling rocky, uneven trails. It also features the Altra’s Original FootShape™ fit and zero-drop platforms that keep your heel and forefoot level.

#4769. Here’s what happened in crypto today

Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.

Today in crypto, Binance received preliminary approval to establish regulated digital-asset operations in Bhutan’s Gelephu Mindfulness City, where it plans to create an Asia hub for Binance users. Bitcoin whales have added about 121,000 BTC since the end of September, defying historical year-end selling patterns, and the EU’s securities watchdog plans to make it easier to verify which crypto companies are authorized to operate in the bloc.

Binance has received in-principle approval from the Gelephu Central Bank (GCB) to establish regulated digital-asset operations in Bhutan’s Gelephu Mindfulness City (GMC).

Binance signed an agreement on a broader partnership and plans for Gelephu Mindfulness City to become an Asia hub for Binance users.

Jigdrel Singay, GMC board director, said “Binance choosing Gelephu Mindfulness City as a base for its Asia operations is an important milestone for what we are building in Bhutan. Our ambition is not simply to attract global companies to establish an entity here. We want them to build real operations, create meaningful jobs, develop talent and transfer capabilities that remain in the country over the long term.

“The in-principle approval is an important first step, and we look forward to working closely with Binance and GCB as Binance completes the remaining regulatory requirements and builds its presence in GMC,” Singay added.

Bitcoin whales are bucking the years-long trend of trimming their balances toward the end of the year. Instead, they are accumulating the cryptocurrency despite falling prices and dwindling unrealized profits.

According to onchain analytics firm CryptoQuant, whales added about 121,000 Bitcoin (BTC) to their holdings between Sept. 30 and Nov. 21, taking their combined balance to nearly 2.95 million BTC, despite a price decline of nearly 30% over the same period.

CryptoQuant defines whales as addresses holding between 1,000 and 10,000 BTC. Unrealized profits across addresses holding at least 1,000 BTC have shrunk 81% to $23.8 billion from $124.7 billion on Sept. 30.

The report, supported by crypto lending platform CoinRabbit, notes that whales have historically reduced their holdings toward the end of the year in both bull and bear markets. Since 2017, whale balances have declined in seven of the nine previous fourth quarters, with 2019 and 2020 being the only exceptions.

Meanwhile, dolphins, a term referring to addresses holding between 100 and 1,000 BTC, have slightly reduced their holdings. The group shed about 15,169 BTC, representing 0.28% of its holdings.

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) is preparing an overhaul of its public crypto register nearly two years after its launch.

The European Union’s securities watchdog plans to replace its manual interim register under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) with a searchable web-based platform around mid-2027, an ESMA spokesperson told Cointelegraph.

The new system will also maintain a version history for individual white papers to provide archives of changes.

MiCA’s transitional period ended in July, which meant that unauthorized crypto service providers had to wind down their EU operations or face multimillion-euro fines or other enforcement action. ESMA’s interim register serves as a public reference point for checking whether a crypto company is authorized in the bloc.

#4760. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4755. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4749. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4742. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.
