#4737. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4733. 8 Best Modular Sofas, Tested And Reviewed by AD's Editors 2026

At one time, a modular sofa looked like it could have been toy furniture—each section clearly delineated. Now, seamless design allows this category of sectionals to look like traditional couches that happen to come apart in easy-to-move pieces. Better yet, this style allows you to customize furniture as your space changes. Whether you’re moving from a small apartment into a spacious four-bedroom and need to grow your seating, or you want to downsize a hulking U-shaped basement sectional into a love seat for a bedroom nook, a modular sectional is the way to go.

Style options abound for sectionals, from the artsy armless Sarah Sherman Samuel design for Lulu and Georgia to the minimalist Castlery and the iconic “Chiclet” silhouette made with injection-molded cushions from Herman Miller.

Moving around the sofa pieces is a cinch with user-friendly connector mechanisms, like slide-in glides and easy-to-configure brackets. It took contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert less than 30 minutes to maneuver the pieces of both her Burrow and Cozey modular sectionals into place. Better yet, most of the best modular sofas on this list come with white-glove delivery, so all you have to do is open the door when it arrives.

You can go as big or as small as you’d like with the Jonathan Chaise Sectional from Castlery, a modular option that starts as a two-seater and builds out to accommodate up to six. “This sofa is incredibly comfortable and feels very well-made,” contributor Rachel Fletcher says in her review. “I’d actually say it’s closer to my mattress in terms of firmness—medium firm to firm—which I very much appreciate. It’s not the kind of sofa you’re going to sink into, quicksand-style, and there’s absolutely no sagging effect.

The minimal, low-slung sofa works great in an understated space and could also appeal to a household with kids and pets. “Castlery does offer swatches and fabric samples, but I went all in without testing first and wasn’t sure what a polyester blend might feel like,” she adds. “Thankfully, it’s very soft. It’s made to resemble wool, but without the itchiness or stiffness. The heathered fabric makes it look expensive and should also help hide stains.”

The Cozey Neptune is a modular sofa that’s a jack of all trades: It can be assembled in less than half an hour, pulls out into a sleeper in two minutes flat, has hidden storage under the cushions, and is available in performance fabrics that protect against spills. Alpert chose the sofa for all those reasons, but what ultimately made the Neptune such a keeper for her was its portability. “I had no problem bringing it into the basement,” she says in her review, despite some tight angles on the landing. “Anyone who lives in a walk-up, has a tight stairway, or has narrow doorways typical of older homes will love this piece.”

Once fully assembled, it proved to be as durable as it is good-looking, treading the line between minimalism and groundedness. “I am very skeptical of couches with cushions on the back because I know that these can collapse, and that will drive me crazy,” Alpert explains. “This back is tightly upholstered, but it comes with three lumbar cushions that have a nice spring to them.” After over a year of nearly daily use from two school-age kids (and their friends), her Neptune still looks pristine.

To make the best use of the Neptune’s full-size sleeper-sofa configuration, Alpert recommends springing for the brand’s Sleep Kit ($270), which includes a topper, fitted sheet, flat sheet, two pillows and pillowcases, and a comforter. All of this fits in the three storage compartments within the seat cushions, a “saving grace” in a house with linens galore, says Alpert.

This rounded-edge, injected-foam modular sofa—affectionally nicknamed “Chiclet”—epitomizes simplicity. It’s the ideal couch if you can’t stand saggy cushions or a wrinkly back. The re-launch of the original 1976 style from Herman Miller sofa designer Ray Wilkes preserves the postmodern splendor of the first edition, but offers new fabrics and colorways, including sunny recycled wool twill and textural viscose-wool bouclé in earthy palettes. Consider this iconic sofa more of an art form than just a place to sit, even if you can build out the two-seat into a spacious six-seat perch.

No need to agonize over whether you’re a left-chaise or a right-chaise person. This reversible design lets you change your mind. Slipcovered cushions provide a relaxed, lived-in look, while its compact footprint—set on a frame made from wood certified by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) to be responsibly sourced—makes it an especially smart pick for apartments, condos, and cozy living rooms. The modules allow you to adjust from a three-piece sectional to a sprawling, six-piece L-shape that can host a party.

Go ahead and dramatically drop down on the Lena sofa; the armless design will keep you from awkwardly hitting the arms. This showstopper from Sarah Sherman Samuel, with artful beam legs and a foam-seat construction, allows for just enough bounce. And because the streamlined silhouette has no sharp corners, you can sit two pieces next to each other for a glorious extended bench seating suited for a large living room.

As seen in Broadway actress Barrett Wilbert Weed’s Brooklyn Heights home, Arhaus is known for statement furnishings, and the Coburn fits the bill for plush lounging in style. Its 22-inch seat depth and down-and-feather–blend cushion fill combine to create a nest that is the ultimate definition of cozy. It’s also a top pick for a family with pets or kids because it comes upholstered in Crypton, an ultra durable fabric that can withstand spills, stains, and snags.

With seven distinct seat pieces, more than 140 upholstery options, and four leg covers, this Serena & Lily sectional wins the customization game. Incorporating the new addition to the Norfolk family, a curved corner piece with a 28-inch seat, creates a sectional with a sleek silhouette worthy of a lounge, especially when you accent the setup with a well-endowed arm chair. Layer on a few throw pillows to create an illusion of a cozy pit for hibernating over the weekend.

The modular design of the Article Beta sectional can work for 13 different configurations, including a love seat chaise and an L-shaped sofa with a chaise. Your living room is truly a canvas to experiment with this sectional, upholstered in a durable blend of polyester, viscose, linen, and cotton that makes it perfect for hosting. While the Beta only comes in three colors—white, cypress green, and gray—you can easily dress it up with a woven throw or a cuddle blanket.

Which Brands Offer the Most Versatile Configurations for Modular Sofas?

Serena & Lily and and Castlery stand out in this respect for offering design-forward options in performance fabrics. Article notably offers many configurations and deep seats.

Are Luxury Modulars Pet- and Kid-Friendly?

Depending on the fabric in question, plenty of modular sectionals are pet- and kid-friendly. Performance fabrics are as kid- and pet-friendly as it gets, designed to be durable, stain-resistant, and easy to clean. Luxury leather sectionals can be less pet- or kid-friendly than those upholstered in performance fabrics, as leather is no match for pet nails, for example. Arhaus notably offers modular sectional styles upholstered in Crypton, which allows liquids to roll off, not penetrate into the seat. The material is also designed to prevent scents from seeping in, making it a go-to for a pet family.

Look for soft, breathable materials like cotton, fleece, or jersey that keep you cozy but still allow for movement. Some performance fabrics wick moisture away and provide added durability.

Your best bet will be to find options with a waistband that won’t dig in and enough room in the thighs. Different styles offer different looks and levels of comfort, and understanding the options can help you select the right pair for your needs. Here’s a breakdown of the most common sweatpant fits.

The relaxed fit is all about breathability and unlimited mobility. These sweatpants offer extra room around the hips and thighs, providing a looser feel throughout the seat. It's ideal for lounging, casual wear, and people who prioritize comfort over a tailored look. Think of it as the ultimate chill-out pant—easygoing and roomy, perfect for a lazy day, lying around the house.

Tapered sweatpants are looser at the top (around the hips and thighs) but gradually get narrower toward the ankle. This creates a more streamlined, modern silhouette for active people who want to move easily while maintaining a fashionable appearance. These pants give off a sportier vibe, perfect for gym sessions, running errands, or looking good while staying comfortable.

Slim fit sweatpants are more form-fitting and cut closer to the body, especially in the thighs and calves. They offer a sleek, minimalist look without being as tight as leggings. They’re ideal for everyday wear and even casual work settings when paired with an appropriate top.

Joggers are a type of tapered sweatpant that features a cuff at the ankle. They often have a more athletic, streetwear-inspired look and are typically made from a thinner material. The hybrid look is favored among athleisure lovers and those who like a sporty, on-the-go aesthetic. Joggers are suitable for running, light workouts, or even running errands.

Features like hidden zippered pockets enhance functionality, especially for travel. Deep side pockets can be super handy for carrying your phone, keys, wallet, earbuds, or small bills while on the go. And if you’re being a couch potato for the weekend, you can stash your remote control or snack in there as well.

Our style team, led by Style Director Christian Gollayan, put each pair through real-life scenarios: casual hangouts, city commutes, travel days, and of course, workout sessions. To keep things fair, we created a rubric and scored them across four key categories: comfort, durability, fit, and versatility.

We assessed how soft and breathable they felt, how well they survived workouts and laundry days, whether they struck the right balance between relaxed and polished, and how easily they transitioned from our homes to the streets. Bonus points went to pairs with performance perks like stretch, moisture-wicking, quick-drying, and anti-odor protection. After all was said and done, we narrowed it down to eight selections that truly stood out.

Sweatpants tend to have a looser fit throughout the leg, while joggers feature a more tailored or tapered fit. This means the legs of joggers will often touch your skin and feel a bit tight if you’ve got beefy calves.

Traditional sweatpants are often made from thicker materials like fleece and have a casual appearance, while joggers can be made from a wider range of materials, including activewear fabrics like nylon or polyester.

Joggers have ribbed cuffs at the ankles and a sportier appearance compared to the relaxed vibe of traditional sweatpants, whereas sweatpants can have either an open design or ribbed cuffs.

Sweatpants have a more relaxed and traditional look, while joggers are designed with a sporty aesthetic, often featuring modern details like zipper pockets and paneling. And because of the difference in ankle cuffs and fit, sweatpants look more casual, whereas joggers look more elevated and sleek.

Joggers are versatile for both athletic and casual wear, while sweatpants are primarily associated with casual lounging and relaxation.

Sweatpants are typically ideal for cozy indoor activities, while joggers can transition from the gym to casual outings due to their sleeker appearance.

#4729. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

#4727. tk Best Ergonomic Office Chairs for a Stylish Workspace (2026)

There’s a reason I am most productive when working from an office, and it’s not the harsh lighting or lack of distractions: It’s my office chair. Previously, I was convinced that “ergonomic” was an empty buzzword used by chiropractors and human resources, but after working from a slew of supportive seats these last few years, I’m a believer. Ideally, office chairs combine a sophisticated aesthetic with a genuinely functional build—and both things can be true in the same design. Maybe that budget mesh chair you picked up from an office supply store does the job, but is it the right culture fit for the very curated aesthetic of your home? Fortunately, I’ve sourced the products that check all the boxes, because you deserve to feel just as productive in your guest room-slash-office space.

Over the years that the Shop AD team has been testing office chairs, often corralling the entire office to take a seat, we’ve expanded our search to curate a high-low selection that includes wallet-friendly picks, but also household names in the ergonomic space, like Herman Miller and Knoll. Our favorite options cosigned by design lovers—we are Architectural Digest after all—and those looking to cure that stubborn tech neck twinge, finally.

Our editors and writers have personally sat on, worked, and Zoomed from each of these picks, at the office and from their home desks. We can attest that not only are they attractive, but they will also provide structural support for your entire body, even through the longest meeting days and tightest deadlines.

As a general practice, the armrests on ergonomic office chairs tend to be bulky. Not so with the Branch Verve Chair, which stands out with its curvy S-shaped supports that give it some space-y, extraterrestrial appeal. The Verve is a newer and sportier model from the brand that set out to modernize dated office furniture (from standing desks to seating), and boasts a sleek breathable mesh back and some slender legs with casters for wheeling around the office.

Contributor Terri Williams notes that sitting for long periods of time is easy thanks to the V-shaped chair design that provides extra lumbar support. At just a hair shy of $600, this chair is also one of the most affordable picks on the list (so it’s a good fit for most people), and one of the most streamlined if you hate the look of typical corporate chairs. The svelte design is why we chose it as our top pick over the AD editor-beloved Ergonomic Chair Pro below, which might not be as visually appealing to the average person. “I can also adjust the height of the softly-padded armrests, the seat depth, the tilt, the tilt tension, and the padded lumbar support,” Williams says of the extra features here that put it into holy grail territory.

There’s a reason the Aeron is Herman Miller’s most beloved and recognizable office chair. The iconic design is truly supportive and customizable to fit your ideal comfort zones, with adjustable offerings from the armrests to the seat itself. The seat is almost bouncy, springing you upright and into the most ergonomic position possible. In her other office chair, shopping editor Audrey Lee sits on a cushion, but states that the Aeron balances support with real comfort. Contributor Zoë Sessums selected hers after a virtual fitting with an ergonomic expert at Herman Miller, who walked her through all the features. (Herman Miller offers an informative online gallery of both imagery and detailed videos if you’re unable to try out a chair in person.) Once the chair was delivered—no assembly required, it literally rolls out of the box—Sessums came away impressed with the power of the patented PostureFit SL back support, which encourages opening up the chest and shoulders, and tilts the pelvis slightly forward. “This chair will save your body,” she says. “It’s easy to see why people invest in supreme desk setups. I would recommend the Aeron chair again and again.”

A bad case of tech neck hates to see the Branch Ergo Pro coming. That’s because the chair’s fully customizable support system is calibrated to ensure that your posture is optimized, even during long hours in one fixed position. It offers 14 points of adjustments total (count ’em!) to keep you comfortable, from the seat height to the headrest for those who are blessed with longer limbs. And compared to the original version reviewed above, this one is far cushier on the seat and armrests, with seven additional points of adjustability. It is slightly less svelte and also slightly more expensive than its predecessor, the original Branch Ergonomic, which our tester Williams also loved for its ergonomic design.

Each of our editors took a spin on the Branch Ergo Pro (read our full review) and came away smitten with the adjustability points and glutes support of this “double-stuffed” chair. “I was especially fond of the arm rests that helped me achieve perfect elbow support with my laptop stand and that the adjustable tilt option gave me the freedom to stretch my back out whenever needed,” commerce editor Audrey Lee noted.

The only drawback is that the Ergo Pro needs assembly out of the box, and the construction process is a bit of a learning curve. Still, everything came together quickly in about 30 minutes or less and was easy enough to complete solo. Since it can be fully disassembled, it’s also a great option for frequent movers.

There’s a lot to like about Haworth’s Breck chair. Lee reported that it arrived swiftly in a large box that was simple to carry inside. The assembly won’t leave you frustrated either. You’ll find instructions on the flaps of the delivery box and Haworth has the same manual available on their website as well as a short video with step-by-step directions. The whole process literally takes less than a couple of minutes before you’re ready to put the chair in action.

Don’t be fooled by the easy assembly process, though, as this office chair is more advanced than meets the eye. “I first received the Breck during a heat wave and appreciated the ultra-breathable backrest which allowed a comfortable amount of air to flow through,” says Lee. But it’s all the adjustable features that stand out to her. Need more tilt? No problem. Wish the armrests were just a tad longer? Easy. Height? Seat depth? Lumbar support? Done, done, and done. And while these are all perks you would expect from a high-priced chair that costs over $1,000, the Breck supplies them at under $500.

A high price tag comes with great expectations—which the Asari chair met completely. Lee appreciated its attention to detail, which included the soft leather, the perfect amount of foam fill in the seat, and a backrest that makes it a treat to sit down and work. “The chair has noticeably softened in a delightful way that’s ultra-accommodating to my dimensions without feeling too sunken in or too stiff,” she says. Unlike leather executive office chairs that can read harsh or overly corporate, the Asari’s look is unparalleled. Lee “absolutely recommends” this chair to anyone looking to splurge on their home office. From physical appearance to practical use, it scores 10s across the board.

It’s rare for a truly ergonomic chair to look as good as the Herman Miller Management Chair does. I chose the brown checkerboard upholstery and stainless steel frame and, not to brag, but my coworkers have since declared FOMO, requesting fun office chairs of their own. Like most Herman Miller options, this chair is very adjustable—the features I focused on customizing to my liking were the seat height and the amount of recline the back can have (which is a lot, actually, I feel like I’m lying down if I push too hard). The back cushion has a bit more firmness to it than the ultra-plush seat cushion, which is great for posture correction and staying focused. While it’s a bit too soft for my all-day liking, I do appreciate the additional padding on days when I know I’ll be mostly stationary. I rarely need to adjust my position, and my knees never fall asleep, something that used to happen quite often in my too-tall office chair. Overall, the management chair is excellent for both a home and office environment. With over a dozen upholstery options, you won’t have to worry about the seat clashing with your existing decor—I find it a stylish midcentury alternative to the often all-black silhouettes that plague traditional offices.

For anyone in need of a custom office chair, Steelcase has solutions. Senior commerce editor Nashia Baker settled on this grey leather version from 23 upholstery options, which allow you to choose from peachy pinks, neutrals, and warm leather hues. The overall silhouette is narrower than most, but the armrests are adjustable and the seat has a soft, gentle glide when maneuvered up or down. Even the wheels are smooth when rolling over floors, carpet or tile. “This chair has literally made the trek with me across the Condé Nast office and on various floors, though I haven’t noticed the wheels wearing or jamming in the months I’ve been testing it,” Baker says. With its stable, upright backrest, the seat discourages slouching, but also has enough give for comfortably sitting hour after hour. At over $2,000, it’s definitely an investment, but for all the custom flourishes, Baker says it’s all worth it.

For those in search of a no frills office chair, this West Elm one is sleek and simple. This is the least adaptable option on this list, in that it doesn’t allow for any other heights or tilts. What it lacks in ergonomic adjustment points, however, it makes up for in design prowess. The sleek stainless steel frame and leather seat make a more eye-catching pair, while the true-ball wheels roll smoothly and without catching on the carpet in the AD office. This is definitely for those who prefer a firmer seat and I liked how upright this office chair felt, like it was almost correcting my posture while encouraging a better sense of productivity. My colleague, shopping editor Audrey Lee, however, wasn’t a fan, stating that it was too firm and didn’t love that the seat doesn’t swivel. “It’s a beautiful chair, and looks much more expensive than the price suggests,” Lee says. “It’s a divisive option, but the straightforward make is something I’d prefer to have at home, when all of my distractions are nearby, and I need the chair to do the heavy-lifting of forcing me to lock in.”

Branch’s Softside chair is a fully upholstered take on their more technical office chairs. It’s still as intuitively designed as the brand’s other chairs with its adjustment points (removable arms, adjustable height, and tension recline), two back heights, and caster wheels, but think of this as your at-home companion to the Ergonomic Pro. Brighter upholstery—I’m partial to the skylight blue—also helps to cheer up a workspace suffering from too much black and grey.

The iconic Danish brand HAY has made a number of noteworthy pieces, but we’re drawn to this amply cushioned roller chair. Dating back to 2009, the 155 Task Chair has two styles: standard and soft. The latter has foam padding and batting that keeps you supported through hours-long meetings. At 20 pounds, it’s a relatively lightweight item, and it conveniently arrives fully assembled for a fuss-free setup process. Plus, the curved seat is one of several ergonomic elements. The chair has a tilting mechanism and gas lift to adjust the angle and height of the seat. This is one of many chairs in HAY’s best-selling About a Chair collection, developed by award-winning furniture designer Hee Welling.

Introduced in 2021, the Zeph Chair is a collaboration between Herman Miller and Berlin-based design firm Studio 7.5. It also went on to earn one of AD’s 2022 Cleverest Awards, with editors noting its midcentury-modern design and ergonomic form for lower back support. The kinematic mono-shell is the most striking feature, a contoured seat and back with voids for a futuristic look. “Even better, the playful chair’s seat is made of 50% post-consumer recycled content and zero fabric waste,” adds Sessums. If you anticipate spending hours upon hours in this chair, we recommend the optional seat pad and arm rests for added comfort. Another thing to feel good about? The polymer shell is easy to clean with a damp cloth, and the 12-year warranty gives you extra peace of mind about investing in a relatively splurge-y item.

Louisa Pierce and Emily Ward of AD100 firm Pierce & Ward have been trusted to design homes for celebrity clients like Dakota Johnson and Emma Roberts, and their collaboration with West Elm shows their vintage-inspired, quiet luxury aesthetic. This button-tufted, swiveling office chair will instantly ground your space. It’s sophisticated and substantial, and the adjustable height lever is located under the seat. If the in-stock upholstery isn’t for you, there are 74 options to customize your chair. So, if you’re working from your living room or the office, you should feel right at home—a concept Pierce and Ward considered while designing their firm’s new Los Angeles studio. As Ward previously shared with AD, “There’s just a different kind of energy when a workspace feels like a home.” Keep in mind this is a limited-edition product, so it’s best to nab it ASAP.

One of the newest models from Swiss furniture manufacturer Vitra, the Mynt Task Chair is a thoughtfully designed, minimalist option for a modern office. Because of the slim profile, this would work well in a home office with a versatile, space-saving desk like the Pierce Wall Desk from West Elm. The natural oak veneer backrest, armrest, and seat is our preferred colorway, but the upholstered styles provide more cushioning, thanks to the polyurethane foam and polyester fiber fill. The responsive design adjusts the seat based on your movements (a.k.a. no manual adjustments needed), and the patented tilt mechanism is hidden within the aluminum frame. Pair it with an oak-stained desk to complement your chair, while also bringing more natural texture to a home office setup.

For the midcentury aesthetes, Arhaus’s leather pieces are contemporary takes on nostalgic silhouettes. Case in point: the Kirsten Faux Leather Desk Chair, an ergonomic approach to a classic leather seat, complete with rounded edges. It can easily find a home in an earth-toned office with a walnut-stained desk, and the antique brass legs add another natural hue to the design. And while it may look like it hails from a different era, there are plenty of updated features, such as the hydraulic lift to change up the height of the seat. Four sturdy, powdercoated aluminum legs are designed to endure long days at the office. And if you’re drawn to the shape of curved back and seat, the brand’s Kirsten collection includes dining chairs and stools. We like the faux leather upholstery, but Arhaus also makes this office chair with green performance velvet and white textured performance weave if you want try other options.

Our commitment to bringing you quality seat recs is well documented, and finding an office chair that is comfortable, well-made, and easy on the eyes can make a world of difference in how you feel while you’re sitting in a seemingly endless one-hour meeting. The Shop AD team thoroughly vets items before including them in our roundups, and we test nearly everything we write about—office chairs being no exception. I, alongside our broader team of writers and editors, tested more than 30 chairs combined to pull together these rankings, with only a few making the cut in our best-of list. I’ve yet to find a stylish, non-bulky gaming chair that meets our standard, and several other generic Amazon picks just didn’t feel elevated enough to make our list of chairs that would suit a design lover—though they may tick the boxes from a purely practical standpoint. Our reviews are always thorough, in-depth, and honest, even when we’re noting how a chair may have fallen short.

Weary workers can rest assured that every pick on this list has been hand-picked and personally vetted by us. Our well-rounded list includes design head-approved picks (Herman Miller! Knoll! Steelcase!) with more approachable best-sellers on Amazon (like Branch) sprinkled in, with top priority going to picks that had a warranty of at least seven years and merged great design with adjustability and comfort.

Over the years spent testing, we’ve also delisted picks from Article, Haworth, Herman Miller, Flash Furniture, Steelcase, Flexispot, and Humanscale that either felt not ergonomic enough for an office setting or didn’t feel like the most superlative choice for their price bracket compared to their peers. The Article Svelti is armless, for example, while the Steelcase Gesture had a stiff backrest and a tedious assembly process. An older version of the Branch Ergonomic has been replaced with the brand new Branch Ergonomic Pro, which was tested by several of our editors.

Whether from the desks of the Condé Nast offices or from home setups, the Architectural Digest team has spent weeks (sometimes months or years) sitting in, working from, and recording their thoughts on the best office chairs. I am a firm believer that the chair makes the workplace, and my fellow editors agree, assuring that each of these chairs met a specific set of criteria—which I’ve outlined below—in order to pass the qualifications to be included in this article.

Delivery and assembly: Straight out the gate, did the chair arrive within the guaranteed delivery window? And if you had to assemble it, was it relatively easy to do so or did it come with a tough-to-parse manual and 100 parts?

Dimensions: Apartment dwellers know better than anyone that being conservative with floor real estate isn’t a want, but a need. That’s why our reviews provide exact measurements for the styles we tested and any notes on whether we thought a chair might not be a good fit (literally) for a modest-sized workspace.

Rating the experience: A chair that’s both easy on the eyes and on the tush is our number one priority. What was your first impression of the chair? Does the design fit a clear aesthetic? Is it meant to be ergonomic? How do the materials perform, and do they seem durable? How did you feel after a full work day and week? Does it include any fun details that may not be obvious at first glance? Our reviews were crafted to give insight on why a chair could be the right one for your 40-hour work week.

What to keep in mind: Everyone has different ideas of perfection—which is why each chair also has a section detailing what a potential buyer should keep in mind. For example, if assembly was particularly difficult, if the chair had special care instructions, and if the design seemed polarizing, we made note of all that.

Editor’s Note: We recently de-listed the Article Svelti office chair due to it being armless in favor of more supportive options.

What Features Should I Look for in an Office Chair?

Our experts—TikTok’s favorite neurosurgeon, Betsy Grunch, MD, FAANS, FACS and Gainesville Physical Therapy's Kristy Basinger PT, CHT—agree that your back rest should be made from breathable material such as mesh for better air circulation, decreased perspiration, and greater comfort overall. Your seat is another important component for gluteal support that should have adequate padding consisting of dense foam or similar materials. Adjustability for different body types is crucial no matter which new chair you choose, so you can ensure your feet are positioned flat on the floor and arms set at a 90-degree angle.

Like any investment piece of furniture, you get what you pay for. There’s a lot of science that goes into crafting a comfortable and supportive office chair that you can actually be productive in. Ergonomic design, smooth movement, textiles, and manufacturing costs all combine to set the price point. Office chairs are so expensive because you’re not only investing in a chair, but also making an investment in your physical health. We spend at least eight hours a day in these seats, and they can dramatically affect our posture, joint health, and mobility. You may not notice the benefits of a great office chair, but you’ll definitely remember your discomfort in a bad one. Of course, there are budget-friendly options, like the Haworth Breck chair that we tested, which comes in above $400.

How Long do Office Chairs Typically Last?

High-quality office chairs typically last between seven and 10 years, which is why we prioritized picks that offer a lengthy warranty to cover the majority of this period. Cheaper office chairs have a much shorter lifespan, typically just a few years. Non-performance fabrics and leather seats will show their age more than performance materials that are better equipped to handle stains, scratches, and general wear and tear. You’ll know it’s time for a new seat when the customizable features—such as armrests, height, and seat position—start to wear out and aren’t as easy to adjust.

What Are the Differences Between Office Chair Styles?

Task: As the name suggests, task chairs are designed for specific tasks. Think of these chairs as short-term, minimal seating for quick bursts of work. They often have a less padded, simpler design and less support than true ergonomic office chairs that are designed for full days. Branch describes these seats as, “Task chairs embrace simplicity in their design, often characterized by a streamlined appearance. They prioritize functionality over excess features, aiming to deliver a no-frills seating solution that's easy to maneuver and adjust.” In this list, the Fritz Hansen Series 7 chair is a high-design task chair.

Executive: An executive office chair typically features a plush seat, high back, and ample spine support to keep you comfortable throughout the entire workday. You’ll find that these chairs offer more adjustment points and customization, like the 14 points on the Branch Ergonomic Pro we tested. Executive chairs come in a variety of materials and silhouettes, from Herman Miller’s signature Eames Aluminum Group chair to the brand’s more futuristic Aeron chair.

Gaming: The most specific type of office chair, gaming chairs have a very distinct shape. Usually with wide shoulders and an ultra-high back that supports your head and neck, gaming chairs prioritize lounge-style comfort without sacrificing ergonomic support. Most include a neck pillow and a lumbar pillow for additional padding and support. While the back is not as adjustable as some office chairs, gaming chairs offer additional customization points on the armrests and base.

Your office chair is just a piece of the puzzle when it comes to outfitting your WFH setup. Brands like Herman Miller, Steelcase, and Branch all offer great desks, filing cabinets, and bookcases to help fill your workspace with design-minded pieces. For those who value flexibility and ergonomic support, look to Branch for our top-tested seats and sit-to-stand desks that can withstand all-day, everyday use. For the midcentury obsessed, there’s no better place to find retro pieces than Design Within Reach. Essential brands like Eames, Knoll, and Vipp are all featured alongside some more modern favorites like Audo Copenhagen, HAY, and Tom Dixon. While we may not be able to channel the Scandinavian vacation policies, we can infuse our workspaces with more of their colorful minimalism to combat that three o’clock slump. If you prefer something more sculptural than corporate-leaning, Lulu and Georgia offers curved stone desks, upholstered seats, and plenty of desk accessories to incorporate more personality. For a full rundown of where to buy office furniture, read our guide here.

Across our vast library of home tours, we’ve noticed a few recurring characters for home offices that designers reach for again and again. Herman Miller, a favorite of our team as well, appears countless times. The retailer, having reached midcentury-modern icon status, is almost instantly recognizable. The aluminum frames, channeled leather upholstery, and wooden details elevate a home office while still providing tested ergonomic support. Jeff Goldblum’s California home boasts the brand’s Eames Aluminum Group chair, and Kevin Hart’s West Hollywood office features the Eames Executive Chair. Design Within Reach is another retailer designers frequent. Other midcentury staples can be found here too, like Knoll’s Morrison chair, the Vipp453+ Swivel Chair (which we’ve previously tested, but removed in favor of office chairs with more ergonomic features), and the Saarinen swivel chair (as seen in Margot Robbie’s production offices).

Does My Office Chair Need Lumbar Support?

Whether you’re sitting in your office chair eight hours a day or just here and there, yes, you need lumbar support. We’re all familiar with the aches that come when sleeping on a sofa for the night or after a long-haul flight, and proper back support helps to mitigate that pain and protect your spine in the process. According to our experts (Betsy Grunch, MD, FAANS, FACS and Gainesville Physical Therapy's Kristy Basinger PT, CHT, cited above), a proper-fitting desk chair is one of the cornerstones of postural health. People who sit for long hours in a poorly adjusted chair will experience neck, back, shoulder, and hip pain. This can trigger headaches, lack of concentration, and compression of the discs in the spine. Low back pain is one of the main reasons for missed days at work, so it’s essential to choose a chair that supports the spine. (It’s also not a bad idea to support your overall health and quality rest with a good mattress for back pain.)

#4725. The Best Walking Shoe Black Friday Deals: Save Up to 63% on Sneakers Our Editors Swear By

Shop favorites from Brooks, New Balance, Dr. Scholl’s, and more.

Walking is a low-impact workout that boosts your heart rate, supports mental health, and is far easier on your joints than running. The catch? All those miles still add up, which means your shoes really matter.

Shop Walking Shoe Black Friday Deals on Amazon

Over the years, our team of editors has tested hundreds of shoes, so we can recommend only the best styles for walking, running, cross-training, and more. Supportive, cushioned walking shoes aren’t cheap, and many of our editors’ favorites cost more than $100—but you don’t have to pay full price because our editors found Black Friday discounts on some of our top picks.

I’m a shopping editor who tracks deals for a living, and right now, you can save up to 63 percent on top-performing brands like Brooks, New Balance, and more. With proven cushioning, stability, and comfort, shop the shoe deals that Women’s Health editors genuinely wear and recommend below.

After testing dozens of walking shoes for our 2026 Fitness Awards, the Adrenaline GTS 25 took the top spot for its near-perfect balance between cushioning and stability. That comfort starts with the 25’s updated midsole, which feels plusher than previous models without losing an ounce of stability. It still features the brand’s signature GuardRails technology—firmer along the sides and softer through the center—to gently lock in your stride.

The upper and outsole of the Glycerin Flex are both made from super bendy materials that give the shoe an almost barefoot feel. We’re big fans of this shoe for walking, long periods of standing, running, and plyometric workouts. It's incredibly versatile, thanks to ample nitrogen-infused cushioning and a flexible midsole. The FlexZone technology—a strategically placed groove in the center of the shoe’s outsole—helps enhance the shoe’s flexibility and allows the foot to move naturally.

If versatility is your priority, the Brooks Ghost 17 delivers. With upgraded nitrogen-fused cushioning, the latest version packs even more padding than the Ghost 16. Impressively, the higher heel stack doesn’t feel too squishy or wobbly. It’s a great do-it-all shoe for long walks, standing all day, and running.

The soft midsole offers the just-right level of give, absorbing impact without feeling too soft or marshmallowy. Plus, the breathable air mesh upper adds to the barely-there feel, and the plush ankle collar doesn’t chafe or rub at all.

This TikTok-famous sneaker reigns supreme for walking and has earned a spot in our guides to the best platform sneakers and best travel shoes for good reason: it delivers all-day comfort without looking overly athletic. The 1.5-inch platform gives this shoe major style points, elongating the legs and giving a little extra height without that heavy, clunky feel some platform sneakers have.

Plantar fasciitis and the heel pain that comes with it can quickly halt your walking workouts. The 2025 WH Fitness Award-winning, best overall plantar fasciitis walking shoe, Brooks Women’s Adrenaline GTS 24, delivers stability and support to keep you (and your plantar fascia) feeling good over time.

The New Balance 608 V5 Trainer has over 38,000 Amazon reviews, and for good reason. The brand integrated its signature ABZORB midsole, designed to reduce joint impact during walking through its cushioning and compression resistance. Plus, they come in narrow, standard, and wide sizing.

For those who appreciate a good slip-on shoe, the Skechers Go Walk Flex Azriel’s lightweight, breathable mesh upper is great for sweaty feet. The ultra-cushioned midsole also offers great arch support.

"This is a solid no-frills walking shoe that’s perfect for errands, quick hot girl strolls, or for walking your dog," says associate style and reviews editor Shannen Zitz. "I love that it slips on easily while still having the appearance of a classic sneaker with bungee laces that never come undone.”

If your main problem is overpronation or supination, the New Balance 1540v3 will lock your feet down. The brand integrates its "Rollbar stability post system," designed to prevent your ankles and feet from rolling inward or outward. On top of that, dense foam is in the midsole for added arch support, while the collar is tough for ankle security. Despite its firmness, the EVA foam remains plush. Extra-wide sizing is available to accommodate a variety of foot types (in addition to narrow, standard, and wide).

Diana Rogers, DPM, a podiatric foot and ankle surgery specialist in Crystal Lake, Illinois, and Casey Pidich, MD, a podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon based in the Bronx, New York, both recommend Hoka's Clifton series to patients for arch support, so you know it's a good one.

Pidich loves that the design encourages great form—the sole ensures that your feet rock off the ground rather than push off your toes. Rogers specifically recommends the shoe to her patients with plantar fasciitis (a condition that causes arch pain) for this exact reason. "The lightweight feel of this shoe propels feet forward rather than making them do extra work," she says.

Lined with mesh for ultra-breathable comfort, the Pegasus is a winner thanks to its slim, low heel that helps maintain a smooth walking cadence. We love that the 42 is lighter than the previous model and has a curvier toe box that gives more toe spring, a smoother ride, and a roomier fit.

Asics is considered a classic, all-around great brand for walking, especially if you struggle with overpronation (ankles that roll inward) or have flat feet. The Gel-Kayano 32 has thick foam borders on each side to encourage proper alignment and walking gait. Deep heel cups also help keep arches supported—there’s a reason this shoe made our best plantar fasciitis walking shoe guide.

#4718. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4713. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”
