#4711. 10 Best Sectional Sofas That Are Actually Stylish, Tested (2026)

As former AD editor Benjamin Reynaert puts it, sectionals allow for “a level of customization akin to bespoke furniture, but without the high costs that come with building a piece from the ground—or sofa leg—up.” Sectionals, more than standard sofas, have a kind of chameleonic style that can adapt just as easily to a basement movie room or the family den. But deciding between the right sectional versus a regular old sofa can still be tough.

If you’re worried that sectionals can lean a bit stodgy or will have trouble squeezing into tight spaces, we’re here to ease your mind with some of our team’s first-hand findings from years of sitting, napping, and binge-watching on the best sectional sofas around. Whether you’re looking for a chaise to stretch out on or a corner piece to anchor your media room, there’s a versatile silhouette just waiting to be brought home. Shop our favorite plush, sculptural picks and sleek, midcentury classics below.

Benchmade doesn’t stop at sending fabric swatches. The company will send you a true-to-size printouts so you know exactly what you’re getting, among more than 125 material and fabric combos of your choosing. That way, you can go beyond visualizing how the Modern Vintage sofa will fit in your space. The brand’s recently launched Vintage collection is for those of us who pine for retro designs but don’t want to spend the hours thumbing through Facebook Marketplace for a secondhand option. The line offers midcentury modern-inspired designs in patterned prints from the likes of Kravet and textile house Pollack. Contributor Noah Kaufman chose the plaid upholstery seen here from Pollack (which is available later this month) and a silhouette with sled legs to fit with his Victorian home’s aesthetic. “In a home with a more midcentury aesthetic, or one that uses more pronounced colors and patterns, it would fit right in,” Kaufman says, noting that the sofa reminds him of the couch in his childhood home.

Despite being known for budget-friendly bamboo and breezy linen bedding, Quince’s recent foray into furniture met our team with equal parts enthusiasm and curiosity. Handmade in North Carolina, where some of the best American furniture hails from, the pieces are designed to be home staples with a timeless aesthetic and for those who aren’t willing to shell out five figures for a sectional. After years spent with a well-loved, second-hand grey sofa, audience development manager Emma Tubbs knew it was time for an upgrade. Enter: Quince’s modern silhouette, the Ashford Deep Seat Chaise Sectional in the performance velvet. “When I found this Quince piece, I was immediately drawn to the gorgeous, deep brown velvet, but the deep seat is really what sold me,” she says. “I love being able to cozy up and lie down on a couch, and in my opinion, there's nothing worse than a narrow sectional.” With a 28-inch seat depth and cushions filled with high-density foam and a feather/down blend, this sofa is meant for all-day comfort. Her one critique: Tubbs notes that while the seat is supportive and plush, the back cushions easily lose their shape and need fluffing after every nap. That said, “the overall construction feels solid and well-made, and I’ve already taken many naps on the couch and woken up refreshed and without any back pain,” she says.

Velvet isn’t always the right upholstery choice for those looking for durability, but the brand’s performance velvet easily withstands spills and pets, needing just a spot clean when you notice a stain. Overall, Tubbs notes that it’s great for game nights just as it is for sick days and rainy weekends spent reading indoors. Even her dog gives it the thumbs up: “While we’re trying to limit our 80-pound very hairy German Shepherd’s access to the new couch, it does warm my heart that the couch can comfortably accommodate all three of us sprawled out.”

Castlery’s Hamilton sectional has a classic design with its tapered arms and boxy shape, and it also happens to be a sleeper sofa. Suiting a more modern or traditional aesthetic, the sectional keeps its structure while still being a crazy comfortable place to lounge around. “My partner and I are true couch people and love to lie around, so getting another sectional was the obvious choice,” says contributor Susie Plotkin. Plotkin goes on to describe this couch as wildly comfortable, and having the kind of silhouette that makes her living room look more polished than it is. It won’t be your living room’s signature piece of decor, but for those looking for a sectional that can easily adapt to their ever-evolving design style, the Hamilton might be for you.

The perk of having a sleeper sofa and a sectional in one is that there is plenty of room to spread out. And for those short on closet space, the chaise lifts up to reveal a storage compartment underneath. But unlike other jack-of-all-trades furniture pieces, this one delivers in just two boxes. Plotkin opted for white-glove delivery, and the entire couch was assembled and ready for a movie night in under an hour.

Like most sleepers, the built-in, memory foam mattress may not compare to your plush bed setup, but Plotkin insists that guests have touted the Hamilton’s comfort, night after night. “We’ve already had people sleep on both the pull-out mattress and directly on the chaise; both got glowing reviews,” she says. “The middle seat is a hair stiffer than the others because of the pullout mattress, but even that is very lounge-able. It feels well-made and durable, and because the high-density memory foam cushions retain their shape, the couch doesn’t sag.” Overall, Plotkin is extremely pleased with her sectional, especially the way it's held up against her two very rambunctious kittens (and their claws). The performance upholstery is stain-resistant and has a subtle texture that adds depth to the otherwise all-white look. Since she doesn’t have a guest room, she was looking for a versatile piece—“not just any sleeper sofa, though, a seating unicorn: a stylish, comfortable, non-bulky sleeper sectional” for her space. “It didn’t even occur to me to look for storage—I was already being greedy with my requirements, so when I found the Hamilton, it skyrocketed to the top of the shortlist,” Plotkin adds.

The Burrow is a family-friendly addition to your living spaces no matter what kind of square footage you’re working with. This three-piece sectional that’s just slightly larger than a loveseat is especially accommodating for smaller layouts and thoughtfully designed with the flexibility to tack on more seating (an ottoman, chaise, or extension here or there) as your family or space changes. The sofa’s stain-resistant upholstery, solid plywood frame, and CertiPUR-US–certified foam base also ensures lasting durability and high-quality comfort. The brand also offers a one-year warranty to give you a bit more peace of mind.

Contributor David Kaufman placed it an entryway area of his home and called it “a great starter sofa for a first home or apartment that you won’t have to send to a landfill when you’re ready to move.” He noted that it falls on the firmer end, but vouches that it’s still a comfy crowd-pleaser among the family. “It’s especially well sized for the twins to curl up in with a friend.”

The Arhaus Coburn reclining sectional is a blocky, yet modernized option (we love the exaggerated seams) for anyone looking for a comfortable recliner that’s trimmed of all the bulk of the Lay-Z-Boys from the early aughts. “The couch is exceptionally comfortable and plush, especially when you use the reclining feature,” says AD contributor Blake Bakkila, who cautions that when you’re not using it in recliner mode, it doesn’t provide as much shoulder or neck support. Another perk of the sofa is its kid-friendly surface, put to the test by Bakkila’s toddler. “The kitchen (and his beloved berries) are a quick sprint from the couch, and we’ve never noticed any stains,” Bakkila adds. It does need ample inches of clearance at the back in order to recline, so it would be better suited for floating furniture layouts rather than a room where it would need to be placed against a wall. Note that this sofa also needs to be plugged into a power source or equipped with battery packs to use the reclining features.

Thuma made a name for themselves with easy-to-build bed frames which lock into place via well-crafted Japanese joinery, though they quickly followed that up with bedroom furniture like nightstands and other modular shelving arrangements. Their most recent launches have positioned Thuma as a brand to know for beautiful furnishings in every room of the house, starting with their new modular sofas. Enhanced with additional lumber support and enforced with liquid-coated steel, these pieces are sturdy and also elegant, with commerce partnerships manager Evan Russum giving them top marks for style and design alone.

“This couch stood out to me because it avoids the bulky, overstuffed look a lot of sectionals lean into,” Russum says. “Instead, it feels streamlined and modern, with modular pieces that clip together in a seamless way that echoes the bed frame’s design ethos.” He noted that there is plenty of room to sprawl out for his lanky 6’5 frame and that despite its delicate ivory color, the couch hasn’t seen any scratches from his cat, snags, or noticeable wear from daily use.

Interior Define’s Sloan sectional offers more customization options than the traditional furniture brand. Choose from dozens of upholstery materials (and colors!), various seat depths, cushion fills, and even leg styles. The personalization is largely why contributor Malia Griggs chose this sofa for her living room. “I really do love this couch. If you enjoy tailoring your décor to your taste, are willing to pay a bit more for quality, and have the patience for a made-to-order process, this is a wonderful sectional—especially for a smaller space (and even with cats),” she says. Having stretched out on the chaise for movie nights, naps, and even one full night, Griggs touts the sofa’s firm yet cozy seat and durable upholstery.

Even with two rambunctious cats, the sofa has held up against spills, stains, claws, and even one poorly timed hairball. “The sectional has held up surprisingly well against their havoc—wrestling on the chaise, treating its sides like a scratching post, and near-constant shedding absolutely everywhere,” Griggs elaborates. She also says that a soft-bristle brush helps maintain the velvet texture and disguises any aggressively clawed areas. “While I wouldn’t call velvet a low-maintenance upholstery choice (it definitely attracts lint and pet hair), it has performed better than I expected,” she says. “Velvet has a short, dense pile that doesn’t snag the same way as my previous chenille sofa—so even when my cats do go to town with their claws, the fabric doesn’t show damage as obviously.”

“We were inspired to create 7th Avenue to solve for a frustration we kept hearing from customers: Finding a sofa that was both beautifully designed and genuinely practical for everyday living was surprisingly difficult,” the brand’s co-founder and CEO Billy Shaw previously told AD. The result is ultra-modular pieces like this chaise sectional, complete with water-repellent and stain-resistant fabric upholstery that are removable and washable (and replaceable if you ever want to mix it up).

Similar to the chaise sectional, this sectional sofa from 7th Avenue promises modularity and water-resistant and stain-repellent properties. The construction is modular, of course, but contributor Meg Kernahan explains how the overall look can coordinate with virtually any interior design. “This sectional has a very versatile look that can work with many different styles,” she shares in her review. “The sleek, no-frills design makes it a perfect backdrop for other elements in the room to stand out. My style leans organic modern with a touch of midcentury, and it blends with my aesthetic well.” Kernahan selected a chocolate brown color, in the hopes that the dark hue and stain-resistant fabric could conceal any marks left behind by her two young kids and dog. She notes that while it’s not completely water-resistant, it can easily repel a splash of water, and that it’s easy to remove the cushion covers and throw them in the wash.

Kernahan calls this couch “incredibly comfy” and says her family has taken several naps on it. “My husband and I can each lie down on either side of the couch at the same time without having to drape our legs over each other (we’re both about 5' 8"), so there is plenty of room to sprawl out and get comfortable,” she says. “It’s notably deep enough for a full night’s sleep (or a solid nap), especially with the back cushions removed.” And after a month of testing (and sleeping) on it, she hasn’t noticed any sagging.

Comfort and natural materials are top priorities for Sixpenny, which rebranded in 2020 to develop eco-friendly pieces with slipcover upholstery. Their feather down is ethically sourced, and the down alternative fill is made with vegan poly fibers. Our team has tested dozens of sectionals, but contributor Zoë Sessums argues this might be the comfiest she’s ever tried. “You can really sink into the seats, yet the cushion filling bounces right back,” she writes in her review. “It feels durable and well made, especially all the stitching on the slipcovers.”

Two years after bringing it home, Sessums says “all the cushions still have so much oomph” and continue to feel supportive—even after cats, dogs, small children, and tall overnight guests have all comfortably used this couch, without causing any damage. “This sofa feels nearly indestructible!” Sessums adds. Even more, her guests often ask if she purchased a new couch because she’s rearranged the units to create different configurations over the years. “Currently, I have the sofa set up as a small sofa and two chairs,” she says. “It’s a nice way to refresh your space while being less wasteful. I sometimes wish the depth was slightly shorter since my house isn’t very big, but overall it works.”

Pottery Barn has been a trusted source for high-quality furniture for decades, so it’s no wonder they make one of the most comfortable—and dare we say “dreamiest”—sectionals. “The level of comfort that this couch possesses is the stuff of legend,” writes contributor Jaha Nailah Avery in her review. “It’s probably the most comfortable couch I have ever had the pleasure of sitting on. It’s constructed so well, and you can definitely tell that it’s made from premium materials.”

True to its name, the Dream is a standard product with several customizations: two widths, an optional storage ottoman, and 80 colorways to choose from. Avery selected the wider version, and says it fits perfectly in her single-family home with a large living room. “At 172 inches wide, 86 inches deep, and 34 inches high, it is quite long, but it fills the space in a way that makes everything a little more cozy,” she explains. “I also love that you can customize its size. You can pop out one or two of the middle sections to make it smaller, or move the ottoman piece to another section.” Her dog Fievel gives a rave review, too, since the upholstery is gentle on his sensitive skin and easy to vacuum or lint roll his hair.

There are many factors we considered in each of our reviews to give you the insight you need to select the best sectional sofa for your home, including:

Ordering and customization process: Shallow seats or deep seats, armrests or armless, right-facing chaise or left-facing chaise, down seat cushions or foam cushioning, upholstery or leather, L-shape or U-shape—each of the sectionals we tested has possibilities. We also documented the lead times and expected delivery timelines for each model.

Couch delivery and assembly: Curbside or white-glove, fully assembled or DIY. And, if DIY, how many pieces did the sofa arrive in and how difficult was the assembly?

After installation: Here we asked some tough functionality questions of each sectional: Is it practical for a modern home? Is the couch kid- and/or pet-friendly? What are the care and cleaning instructions? And did it look better IRL than in the photos?

Durability and longevity: When possible, we followed up with testers to see if they still stood by their original reviews months or years down the line.

We updated this story for Seat Week 2025 with couches that AD staffers and contributors spent the summer vetting, including a new reclining sofa. Above all else, we prioritized picks during testing that were stylish, comfortable, reasonably easy to assemble, and durable enough not to stain or tear even when pets and children are present. Only picks that earned at least a B grade in our testing (which was appointed according to the factors outlined above) made the cut. Over the last successive updates, we’ve delisted picks from Lovesac and Sundays that felt less elevated than their peers for the price point. Meanwhile, a best-selling style from Albany Park that we tested has been retired by the brand as of 2026.

Of course, our homes and apartments can only fit so much seating, so we added a section of runner-up styles that we hope will round out your search for a beautiful, comfortable sofa, no matter what your budget may be. We haven’t tested these models firsthand, but we made sure to choose design-forward styles that are sold at reliable retailers. Most even include customer reviews that offer a glimpse at how these sectionals would hold up in your own home.

Deciding what sectional shape you’re in the market for will help you streamline your decision making. Take into account exactly how much square footage you have to fill, along with what kind of space it will occupy (a family-friendly space with lots of foot traffic will require different kinds of materials than a rarely used guest room, for example).

L-Shaped Sectional: Arguably the most traditional sectional shape, and the one you’ll come across most on this list, L-shaped sectionals are suitable for just about any space. They’re space maximizers—snugly fitting into corner areas and making the most out of your square footage. They also create a shape that can be corralled around a few accent chairs or a statement-making armchair (something like an Eames lounger). If you’re looking for styling inspiration, we’d point you in the direction of this Parisian apartment which coordinates the sectional and wall color to create the illusion of a bigger room, or this Gramercy Park apartment where a sectional sits back in an otherwise open layout.

U-Shaped Sectional: U-shaped sectionals are ideal for larger families looking for lots of seating as well as the perpetual hosts and hostesses, who want party guests to have a spot to kick back. For true U-shape inspiration, look to Stacey Bendet’s Upper West Side abode, where a green velvet U-shape sectional serves as the centerpiece in the designer’s colorful living room.

Curved Sectional: A cousin of the L-shaped and U-shaped sectional, the curved sectional isn’t bound by static lines. At times it takes on a true "U" design, while we’ve also seen configurations take on a snake-like S-shape. Like an L-shaped sectional, some curved sectionals work nicely in corner spots like this one in Pierre Yovanovitch’s Paris office. Curved sofas and sectionals are also unique because they don't necessarily feel out of place in the center of a room, whereas a more angular couch may create an awkward flow. If you think this type of sectional might be your vibe, we'd use the curvaceous seating arrangements in Chrissy Teigen and John Legend's home designed by AD100 designer Jake Arnold as your style inspiration.

Modular Sectional: We consider modular sectionals to be the jack-of-all-trades of the seating world. With a modular arrangement the world is your oyster—want to add more seating to your L-shaped sectional by making it into a U? No problem. Not happy with a sectional all together? Lots of modular designs actually allow you to re-configure your furniture into single and loveseats. Think: Colman Domingo’s impressive Ligne Roset Togo configuration or the Mario Bellini velvet number in this Los Feliz home.

Sofa With Chaise: If you’re not completely sold on the idea of a sectional, a sofa chaise is the perfect middle ground. With this option, there’s no need to agonize over whether a left or right facing chaise works with your space—the detachable chaise allows you to switch it up.

What Features Should I Look for in the Best Sectional Sofas?

Determining the right size sectional for your space is key to a) getting it in the door and b) ensuring that the arrangement doesn’t overwhelm your living room. We would classify three size categories to help you narrow down which to make shopping a little easier on you:

Seat depth—or the distance between the backrest and the outer edge of the seat cushion—is another factor that you’ll want to consider for the ultimate comfort to match your height. There’s no right seat depth, per se, but a deeper-seated sofa is better suited for someone leggier or simply sprawling out, while something more narrow is ideal if you’re looking to sit more upright. Brands like Interior Define also custom make sectionals to your exact depth preference if you have a specific number in mind.

While we’d all like to champion the white couch lifestyle, it’s not always practical if you’re sharing a home with little ones or pets. Thankfully advancements in upholstery tech have developed performance fabrics that promise resistance to spills and durability against everyday wear and tear. You could easily add a luxurious feel to your space with a jewel-toned velvet à la John Legend and Chrissy Teigen or Vanessa Hudgens. But if you’re a traditionalist, you might find inspiration from neutral picks like Ashley Tisdale’s Sixpenny or Taylor Hill’s cloud sofa.

Lately, designers are demonstrating that statement sectionals are something to aspire to. One look at Kendall Jenner’s “grandma-chic” chintz sofa upholstered in Lee Jofa’s Hollyhock Handblock print, under the guidance of AD100 designer Heidi Callier, is an invitation to expand your own floral dreams. (Open Door viewers wouldn’t stop praising the bold design choice.)

A recent report on designers’ couch trend predictions for 2026 are generally pointing to a shift from blocky silhouettes to styles with rounded edges (à la Mario Bellini’s infamous Camaleonda sofa). These bulbous styles owe a lot to the popularity of conversation pits, encouraging banter between seated guests and a comfy, closed-in feel. Postmodern, relaxed silhouettes like the Natuzzi and slouchy Maralunga profiles are also enduringly relevant as cool personas of the sofa world.

When it comes to colorful choices, florals, plaids, and stripes are offered more frequently as ready-to-ship. People are also overwhelmingly gravitating to 1970s colorways and styles that are laid-back and comfy. But unlike something you’d find in an old wood-paneled basement, the upholstery is often applied to modern silhouettes.

#4707. Where Does Caroline Kennedy Live Now? Unpacking the Former First Daughter’s Real Estate Portfolio

She entered the public eye as a little girl living in the White House, but where does Caroline Kennedy live now? The only surviving child of President John F. Kennedy and Jacqueline Kennedy, the diplomat and author has lived in many prominent homes throughout her life, the Executive Mansion being just one of them. Below, we’re unpacking all of the places that Caroline has called home.

An aerial view of the Kennedy Compound in Hyannisport, Massachusetts

In 1956, the year before Caroline was born, her parents paid $45,948 for a home at the Kennedy Compound in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, where JFK’s parents and brother, Robert F. Kennedy, also owned homes. The 4,500-square-foot residence was built in the mid-20s, which is also the period when the famed family first put roots in the area. Born on November 27, 1957, Caroline spent childhood summers at the Cape Cod enclave. It was also where, on July 19, 1986, she married museum exhibit designer Ed Schlossberg.

Caroline Kennedy and Edwin Schlossberg on their wedding day in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts

When Jacqueline died in 1994, the property went to Caroline and her brother, John F. Kennedy, Jr., but reportedly, only John spent his summers there. After he and his wife, Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, tragically died in a 1999 plane crash, the home’s ownership went to Caroline and her children. In 2004, Caroline sold the dwelling to her uncle, Senator Edward Kennedy, for $3 million. “It was sold to the senator to keep it in the family,” family friend Dick Gallagher told the Cape Cod Times. “It will always be the president’s house.”

Caroline spent her first few years primarily living in Washington, DC’s Georgetown neighborhood. In late 1957, her parents paid $82,000 for a brick Federal-style home and tapped designer Sister Parish to decorate its interiors. The Kennedys lived at the circa 1811 property, known as the William Marbury House for the Federalist financier who first lived there, until JFK’s 1961 presidential inauguration. John Jr. was also born during this period. The 5,215-square-foot residence was most recently sold in May 2026 for $6.125 million.

US President John F Kennedy in the Oval Office of the White House with John Kennedy Jr and Caroline Kennedy in 1962

Of course, the next residence that the Kennedys took up was the White House, where they lived from 1961 until President Kennedy’s 1963 assassination. Caroline attended kindergarten in the White House’s solarium along with about 20 other children. She was photographed riding her pony named Macaroni, a gift from Lyndon B. Johnson, on the White House lawn for Life magazine in 1962. The image inspired Neil Diamond to write his hit song, Sweet Caroline. In 2011, Caroline recalled celebrating childhood Halloweens in America’s most famous dwelling: “One of my favorite memories of living here is dressing up in my witch costume and going over to scare my father in his office,” she said.

After JFK’s death, Jacqueline, Caroline, and John moved back to Georgetown, in a $175,000 home known as the Newton D. Baker House, on the same street as their former home in the neighborhood. After less than a year of being hounded by tour buses at the residence, Jackie put the 1794-built Federal-style dwelling up for sale and headed for the Big Apple.

Jackie Kennedy Onassis outside of her 1040 Fifth Avenue home

The family of three moved into a 14-room penthouse apartment on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, which Jacqueline bought in July 1964 for $200,000. The 5,300-square-foot home had five bedrooms, five-and-a-half baths, and views of Central Park and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, where Caroline later worked and met her future husband. The 18-story limestone building was built in 1930 by prominent architect Rosario Candela. The penthouse unit had a library, conservatory, three fireplaces, and a balcony overlooking the park. Caroline lived there until 1972, when she left to attend a boarding school in Massachusetts. Jacqueline called the apartment home until her 1994 death. A year later, billionaire David Koch bought the unit for $9.5 million.

An aerial view of Jackie Kennedy’s Martha’s Vineyard property

In 1979, Jacqueline bought Red Gate Farm, a 340-acre property on Martha’s Vineyard, for $1.1 million. At the time, only a small hunting cabin sat on the grounds. The former First Lady soon built an impressive compound comprised of a Cape Cod–style main house with five bedrooms, a four-bedroom guesthouse, a three-bedroom caretaker’s house, a boathouse, a storage building, two garages, a pool, a tennis court, and a treehouse for her grandchildren.

The property stayed in the family long after Jacqueline’s death. Caroline and Schlossberg’s daughter, Tatiana, was married at the residence in 2017. Two years later, Caroline listed Red Gate Farm for $65 million. “Forty years ago, my mother fell in love with Martha’s Vineyard. When she found Red Gate Farm, it was a perfect expression of her romantic and adventurous spirit,” she said in a statement. “The dunes and ponds and rolling hills of Aquinnah gave her the chance to create a world where she could be so close to nature, close to her family and friends, and, most importantly, close to her beloved books.”

In a letter printed in The Vineyard Gazette, Caroline explained her rationale for the sale. “Being able to raise our children in a place that meant so much to my mother and my brother has kept them close to our hearts. Now that our children are grown, it is time for them to spread their wings, and for us to explore new places.” The diplomat also recalled her pleasant memories at the property over the years: “Together we wove the traditions of summer across three generations — setting lobster pots in Menemsha Pond, entering the Fair and never winning, growing a vegetable garden, bringing home the best shell from the beach every day, getting stuck at the airport when the fog rolled in.”

In 2020, 304 acres of the property sold for $27 million to two nonprofits: the Martha’s Vineyard Land Bank Commission and the Sheriff’s Meadow Foundation. In 2025, it opened to the public as the Squibnocket Pond Reservation. A year later, the Land Bank Commission paid an additional $10 million for a 32-acre portion.

Caroline and Schlossberg still own 95 acres of the property, including the main house and guesthouse.

Caroline and Schlossberg primarily raised their children, Rose, Tatiana, and Jack, in an apartment on Park Avenue on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. The dwelling has six rooms and was described in a 2009 NBC News report as “a low-key place covered with books and decorated with slip-covered sofas.” The couple seems to still own the residence.

Following Tatiana’s tragic death to cancer in June 2026, Jack told People that his parents had moved in with Tatiana’s husband to help take care of their grandchildren, aged two and four years old. “My parents are grandparents, but they’re really playing the role of new parents right now,” Jack told the outlet. “They live with my niece and nephew and take care of them every single day… they’re all living in the same apartment.” Three months before her death, Tatiana and her husband bought an Upper East Side co-op unit near her parents’ apartment.

#4704. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”

#4698. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4697. Where Does Martin Short Live? Exploring the Comedian's Real Estate

He hails from Canada and moved to Hollywood in the mid-1980s. So where does Martin Short live now? The comedian and actor got his start in showbiz in the early 1970s in Toronto, where he was based until he joined Saturday Night Live for the 1984-85 season. Shortly after, Short put down roots in Los Angeles, where he still primarily resides. Although the actor’s work has repeatedly brought him to New York City—SNL, his Tony-winning stage work on Broadway, and the Upper West Side-based series Only Murders in the Building—there have not been any reports of Short investing in real estate in the Big Apple. Though he has long been a naturalized US citizen, Short maintains a vacation property in his native country.

Read on to learn more about where the comedian has lived over the years.

In 1972, just before graduating from McMaster University in his hometown of Hamilton, Ontario, Short headed to Toronto to pursue acting at the urging of his former classmate, Schitt’s Creek star Eugene Levy. He was quickly cast in his first role in a credit card commercial before auditioning for the musical Godspell; both Short and Levy were cast in the production, which opened just a few days after Levy graduated. Future SNL cast member Gilda Radner, with whom Short began an on-again, off-again relationship, was also in the cast. “By September, Gilda and I were more or less living together full-time at her place, at 77 Pears Avenue, and I was madly in love,” Short recalled in a 2014 memoir. Eventually, Short’s future wife, Nancy Dolman, joined the Godspell cast; the pair started dating in 1974.

For some of this period, Short rented a brick house at 1063 Avenue Road in the Eglinton-Lawrence neighborhood with Levy. The house became a place where comedians gathered for Godspell cast parties and script-writing sessions for the sketch show Second City Television. Radner, Dave Thomas, Victor Garber, Andrea Martin, and John Candy were among the other comedians who frequented the house.

Short and Dolman were married in 1980 and settled in Los Angeles in 1986. They paid $1.3 million for a property in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood and built a Cape Cod-style dwelling with five bedrooms and seven bathrooms. The architectural style was chosen “because that’s what my wife told me we were going for,” Short said in a 2006 Chicago Tribune interview. “Whatever my wife says. I have no involvement… I would say it’s traditional. Very classic, very cozy… I couldn’t live with cold modern design.” In the same interview, the comedian said that a David Hockney painting graces the living room wall. “It’s abstract, but it’s beautiful. It was a gift from a family friend,” he explained. Short also revealed that he has a home theater and a large DVD collection—or at least, he did at the time of the mid-aughts interview.

According to the Los Angeles Times, the home has two stories and is “filled with family photos.” In his 2014 memoir, Short opened up about living in the house alone, following Dolman’s 2010 death. “Some nights, when I'm really missing her, I'll grab a rum and Coke at twilight and sit on the couch on our front porch, or perhaps upstairs, on the balcony off of our bedroom, with the Pacific Ocean in view,” he wrote. The Father of the Bride actor still maintains his longtime home.

Short made his first publicly known real estate purchase in nearly four decades in April 2024. He paid $2.2 million for a midcentury home in Brentwood, Los Angeles. The 1961-built home had been recently renovated when the actor added it to his portfolio. Across 1,859 square feet, the single-story residence has four bedrooms and three bathrooms. Its interiors are contemporary, with white walls, hardwood floors, and beamed ceilings. There’s a living room with a black marble fireplace, a separate guesthouse complete with a kitchenette, a primary suite with a balcony, and French doors throughout that open to the yard, which features a kidney-shaped swimming pool with an inset spa and a deck for al fresco dining.

Short still owns this property, though he doesn’t appear to live there; according to its listing on Zillow, the home is currently available to rent for $8,995 a month. Photos suggest that the actor hasn’t made many changes to the home, either.

The Canadian comedian also has a vacation home in his home country. “As much as I adore the excitement of cities, it’s rural Canada that has always had my heart,” Short said in 2013, when his Muskoka property was depicted on the back of a Royal Canadian Mint $3 collector coin. “I am lucky enough to own a cottage on a lake roughly three hours north of Toronto in a staggeringly beautiful part of Canada, which I’m thrilled to share on this coin I had the privilege to help design.” Short stays at his Lake Rossau cabin, his “all-time favorite place,” every summer. "It's just like heaven up there,” he told Travel and Leisure in 2024. “Ontario has endless lakes — it's just beautiful and idyllic.” The May 2026 documentary Marty, Life Is Short included archival home video footage of Short and Dolman hosting their famous friends, including Levy, Steve Martin, Catherine O’Hara, Tom Hanks, and Steven Spielberg, for summer get-togethers and Christmas parties at the cabin. In the documentary, Short described the property as his version of heaven.

#4696. Splitting in Borderline Personality Disorder

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

Have you ever met a new friend who seemed to think you were too great? You can do no wrong, you’re the first person to ever truly understand them, you’re so much better than their other friends. But then you have a disagreement or miss a birthday party, and they seem to just…turn on you? Now they feel sure that you were only ever kind to them because you wanted something; you’re just like everyone else.

Idealization and devaluation like this are two sides of the same coin—splitting, which is most associated with borderline personality disorder, or BPD. But it, or behaviors that closely resemble it, can also occur in people with narcissistic traits, depression, anxiety, autism, and other conditions. In fact, we all do it to some degree; teenagers are notorious for it. And it happens in all kinds of relationships: friendship, family, professional, marriage or partnership.

Obviously, neither extreme is a complete or fair perception of you. The truth of who you are exists somewhere between the ideal and the devalued, but that liminal space isn’t something your friend has access to right now.

And within that inability to see the space between all-good and all-bad lies the definition of splitting. In all of us, certain cognitive processes go offline when we become dysregulated or lose homeostasis: You don’t communicate well when you’re hungry, you can’t appreciate the beauty of a sunset when you’re angry, and so on. Likewise, when your friend or loved one becomes triggered and splits, their ability to see the nuance of who you are goes offline.

In a way, you each experience a similar betrayal. You’re late coming home from work, and by the time you arrive, your spouse’s overactive threat detection network has them convinced you’re seeing someone else. You don’t really love them. You’ll probably leave. You’re abandoning them.

Of course that’s not what you’re doing. So, you’re likewise blindsided by their response. Your spouse is fuming because you betrayed them, and they have some choice words for you. Every positive aspect of your relationship is read back to you in a negative light. It feels like they hate you.

There is no law that says you must stay in a relationship with this dynamic. However, if you’re committed to it, then equanimity is paramount. Your key to coping is not to internalize either idealization or devaluation. Even though it feels so personal, it’s not about you. It’s about their pain and fear.

It may help to think of splitting as a halted developmental process. Children learn good and bad first, and then they come to understand nuance later. But that learning can be disrupted by a number of childhood experiences, including:

When a person’s emotional development was disrupted in this way, their brain is quick to interpret small things as threats, such as:

It’s not willful, and that’s important for any person who loves someone with BPD to know. In most cases, people with borderline personality disorder experienced feeling chronically unsafe, uncared for, or unseen during an important developmental stage. Their brain is hyper-wired to detect this type of threat and respond defensively.

You’re under no obligation to engage in any relationship that doesn’t work for you. You decide what’s okay for you, and it’s a neutral choice. No one has to be right or wrong. And if a relationship ever involves threats or physical harm, that crosses a line no diagnosis excuses. Leave the situation and get help right away.

If you’re safe and you choose to stay involved: First, know that borderline personality disorder is highly treatable. Recovery and remission are possible and even likely with the right support. And there are a few things you can do to take care of yourself and support your loved one. For you:

And to support your loved one in feeling safe and secure so that they may recover:

Learned safety can rewire the fear that leads to splitting. As people with BPD build a sense of safety in treatment and in trustworthy relationships, the space between all-good and all-bad slowly and increasingly opens up to them.

#4695. 'I Kickstarted My Upper-Body Strength Transformation Using Only A 25-Lb. Bag Of Rice'

"I developed so much discipline that translated into every other aspect of my life."

As soon as I started walking, I was playing a sport. I don’t remember there being a time where I wasn't on a sports team during my childhood. To me, exercise was practice after school and traveling for games on the weekend for whatever sport I was playing. As a teen, in my off-seasons, my mom would beg me to go to the gym with her for fun, but I didn't have much interest in it.

I liked running and endurance-based activities because I felt like they complimented sports pretty well, especially lacrosse, which eventually became my main activity. I ended up being able to play lacrosse in college, where I was first required to start strength training to prepare for the season. While I was in shape for my sport, I couldn’t even lift the bar in the gym, and I was mesmerized by all the different movements that I didn’t really understand.

In the middle of college, everyone was sent home because of the pandemic. I felt far away from my entire life and all my friends, and like there was nothing for me to be doing. There was so much time on my hands, and there was nowhere for me to be.

While sitting at home alone, I had nothing to do besides work out. To pass the time and cope with what was happening, I wanted to exercise, but I felt stuck since gyms were closed.

Then my dad handed me this 25-pound bag of rice from Costco and said, “You can train with this. There’s actually a lot you can do with it.” So I stuffed that bag of rice in a backpack to make it heavy, and I’d use it as a weight. I would put the backpack at the front of my body and do squats. I would use it as a kettlebell for kettlebell swings. I would put it on my back and do walking lunges.

I realized there was a lot I could do at home, but I wanted to try to strength train at the actual gym. I decided that, when I was done playing college lacrosse, I would get serious about a gym routine.

When I graduated from college, I was excited—but so confused—about where to begin. I followed fitness influencers on TikTok who gave workout tips and advice on which movements to try. But I also wanted to make sure all of my information was accurate and science-based, so I started researching online, watching the moves other people at the gym were doing, and reaching out to my old college coaches for tips.

At first, I thought I needed to be running and lifting every day to stay fit, but I soon realized I was over-exerting my body. I started learning more about the basics of strength training and how to work different muscles with compound movements like squats, deadlifts, hang cleans, and more. I also learned how to supplement those movements by doing auxiliary exercises with dumbbells or body weight exercises like curls, lunges, and more.

After a combination of trial and error, researching, and practicing at the gym, I finally found my strength training routine and stride. I started to finally perfect my strength exercises. My confidence was growing so much as a result, which only motivated me to continue. I developed so much discipline that translated into every other aspect of my life.

Even when things got off-routine for me, I could fall back into strength training to find my rhythm again. I know it’ll always be there, giving me structure even when everything else feels unsettled.

When I first started lifting, I was hungrier because I was training more, but I was afraid to eat more. But if you want to build muscle, you need protein and you have to eat! It’s how your body survives and thrives. You need to take care of yourself, and that includes getting enough sleep.

I do not always feel motivated to workout. That’s just how life is. But when I started strength training, I developed so much discipline. Even when I don’t have motivation, that discipline is there now, not just at the gym. Stick with it and allow that habit to form.

It’s honestly true when they say that movement is medicine. When I'm taking care of my body, even if my mental headspace isn't in peak condition, I feel better after movement. It’s not all about hitting personal bests, either. (Though those certainly help!) I might tell myself, “I don't want to go to the gym today, but I will because I know it’s good for me.” Strength training gives me the confidence to know I can do anything I set my mind to.

Nowadays, I strength train four days a week, and I’ll also do a designated cardio day. I base my training on muscle groups.

Each workout will have a main exercise, such as a squat, bench press, or deadlift. Then, I pair them with auxiliary exercises like lunges, quad extensions, hamstring curls, rear delt flies, incline dumbbell bench presses, and more that target smaller muscles.

I try to stay between four to five exercises per workout so I don't overdo it. I like to keep it simple when I write my workout plans. I’ll follow those plans for a certain number of weeks depending on my goals, then I’ll move on from there. I like to keep things interesting for myself to ensure I never get bored, because I want to be able to do this forever.

I used to not be able to hang clean the bar, and once I even dropped it on my knee and ruptured my bursa. It was all bruised, and I was so embarrassed. From then on, I had a real mental block with hang cleans. I told myself, “I’m never going to be able to do a lot of weight.”

Years later, I decided it was about time I face my fear. I worked my way up to being able to put 25-pound plates on each side, coming out to about 100 pounds, depending on the bar. The more I practiced, the easier it became for me, and getting there was a huge milestone.

Any upper-body movements are especially empowering to me. Many people don’t think you can have impressive upper-body strength as a woman. When I was able to work my way up to putting a 45-pound weight on each side for bench presses, coming out to 135 pounds, I felt unstoppable. It was such a big deal to me since I never thought I’d be able to do it. It’s such an empowering feeling to be doing something that a lot of people see as something only men would do.

#4693. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

Black Friday beauty deals are going strong. I’ve already scored savings on skincare deals, LED face masks for my parents, and microcurrent devices for my favorite group chat. But one of the most underrated products to stock up on during this fleeting sales event is shampoo.

Hear me out: From sweaty runs on our walking pads and heat styling to product buildup, we put our precious scalp and strands through a lot. After all, our scalp is an extension of the skin on our face—it sheds dead skin cells, collects dirt and bacteria, and secretes oil and sweat, says trichologist Anabel Kingsley in our guide on how often to shampoo your hair. A great shampoo not only keeps our scalp and hair clean, it also targets our specific cosmetic concerns, such as frizzy hair, maintaining the vibrancy of color-treated locks and pumping up the volume of flat strands.

Just remember that Black Friday ends tonight, November 27. There’s no guarantee there will still be discounts going into Small Business Saturday or Cyber Monday. Given the fast-paced nature of these sales, product inventory is more likely to get low closer to midnight. My suggestion: Since many of these hairstylist-approved, editor-tested shampoos are available on Amazon, you should consider taking advantage of the retailer's signature two-day Prime shipping.

For dryness, humectants and conditioning ingredients such as glycerin, hyaluronic acid, and nourishing oils are your new beauty best friends. They help the hair retain moisture and feel softer and more manageable, says hairstylist Courtney Foster. Cécred by Béyonce and Design Essentials are my go-to picks for hydrating my parched strands.

CeraVe Anti-Dandruff Oil Balancing Shampoo

Design Essentials Honey Creme Cleansing Shampoo 12oz

Now if you like to shampoo after working out, reach for Doc & Glo by tennis star Sloane Stephens. Our features director Rachel Epstein used it after a sweaty Rumble boxing class and loved the results so much she continued using the shampoo and matching conditioner. Beyond the calming peppermint-and-eucalyptus scent that lingered for the rest of the night, her scalp felt balanced. Additionally, her waves are fresher and fuller the next day. Talk about a beauty win! “Because I have dandruff, I still need to use a medicated shampoo here and there, but I’ll definitely continue using this duo,” she says.

How often you shampoo varies based on your lifestyle, how quickly your hair gets greasy, your scalp health, and hair type. However, dermatologist DiAnne Davis, MD, recommends shampooing at least once a week, as a jumping off point. Use your best judgment, but if you’re not totally confident on your cadence, ask your hairstylist.

More than 50 percent of women will experience some form of hair loss, according to the Cleveland Clinic—and taking action is easier than you think. Hair shedding can be caused by hormonal fluctuations, stress, dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis, and genetics (just to name a few). So, you’ll want to ask a dermatologist to get to the bottom of what's causing your thinning. However, getting your at-home routine down pat helps support a healthy scalp—and don’t just take my word for it. "There are certain basic properties of shampoo that can be hugely beneficial if you’re trying to prevent or reduce hair shedding,” says dermatologist and hair specialist James Kilgour, MD, in our guide to the best shampoos for thinning hair.

"The bond-building ingredients are good for maintaining the strength and the health of the hair you have rather than making your hair look thinner—it has less of a role in stimulating new growth by itself," he says.

When I moved from Florida to New York, my scalp was easily irritated and my hair color faded quickly. I thought it was due to testing dozens of beauty products for work. Shampoos with “buildup remover,” “clarifying,” or “chelating” on the label are helpful for removing minerals found in hard water.

#4691. Why Are Addiction and Suicide Attempts Treated Separately?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 28, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

This week I have a lot to be thankful for. Three years ago, I spent Thanksgiving Day in an alcohol and drug treatment center, both eager to leave and afraid to be discharged the next morning. I was one month clean from a devastating, years-long addiction, and I was starting from scratch after leaving my career to save a family I wasn’t sure could forgive me. The urge to suicide, though acute when I entered treatment, had receded to arm's length.

Until last week, I hadn’t reflected on this desperation for some time. Then I got a heart-wrenching call from a friend in recovery. One of the men in our peer group had taken his own life. Like me, he’d endured many relapses, but the personal consequences of his latest setback reached beyond his ability to cope.

I had three reactions—two highly subjective and one objective. As a human, I was deeply saddened. A fellow traveler, in the prime of his life, was taken from his family, unable to disclose his suicidal urges to anyone who might have helped.

At the same time, I understood. As someone who’s attempted suicide twice during relapses in years past, I’d done the same thing as our friend, but I survived. I therefore grasped, at a level not everyone can, why he couldn’t do things differently.

Finally, as a psychological scientist who’s treated addiction and studied substance use disorders and suicide, I was reminded of our field’s slow progress in preventing and intervening with some of humanity’s most pressing personal ailments.

Twenty-five years ago, when I began teaching college courses on addiction, it was already apparent that people with alcohol and substance use disorders are at much higher risk of suicide than the general population. Studies had placed this risk at 10-fold or higher, and little has changed since. Then, like now, alcohol and drugs were implicated in nearly half of suicide deaths.

Given these statistics, it’s perplexing that research on and treatment of addiction and suicide are mostly separate in the U.S., something the Department of Health and Human Services lamented earlier this year. Journal articles on addiction usually don’t mention suicidal ideation or behavior, and journal articles on suicide seldom mention addiction. Why?

Professional training programs in addiction are highly specialized and often independent of more general training programs for mental illness. Moreover, most treatment facilities for addiction are private and operated outside the hospital-based systems of care where we treat other clinical syndromes, such as bipolar disorder, depression, and suicidality.

I’ve worked at and been a patient in both inpatient psychiatric hospitals and treatment centers. Patients who are fighting addiction often find themselves in psychiatric wards, not treatment centers, following suicide attempts. Understandably, staff prioritize suicide risk over addiction, often unaware that the former would never have happened without the latter.

When addiction’s role in suicidal behavior is obscured, referrals to addiction treatment are less likely. This is especially so when patients under-report their alcohol and drug use, which is common in medical settings because patients fear stigma. Ironically, stigma runs deep in medical and mental health settings, something Nora Volkow, Director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, has voiced significant concern over.

Treatment centers often show the opposite pattern as psychiatric hospitals, with stigma toward suicide suppressing its candid discussion, even though the numbers show us that most clients have experienced suicidal ideation, and 40 percent have attempted at least once.

One might expect more openness to talking about suicide in peer support groups for addiction, but local group rules, customs, and personalities often discourage such disclosures. In my experience attending thousands of peer support meetings for addiction over the years, I recall less than a handful of suicide-related self-disclosures.

More recently, I’ve begun attending, as an expert observer, peer support groups for self-harm, suicidal behavior, and related mental health challenges. Although it’s early, I've heard no disclosures of substance use or addiction.

In the U.S., addiction and suicide are the two most stigmatized mental health conditions. My hunch is that peer support groups carry society’s stigma. Joining a peer support group for addiction—a difficult decision for most people—grants participants “permission” to talk about a specific mental health issue, which becomes destigmatized among members. Stigma toward other mental health issues, including suicide, remains unaffected.

The friend who called me last week recruited a suicide expert to address our peer support group. I hope it makes a difference by encouraging members to self-disclose. I, along with a colleague, have also initiated a peer support program that tackles both addiction and suicidality explicitly. I’ll report back another time to let you know how that goes.

Three years removed from my own mental health crisis, I have a lot to be grateful for this Thanksgiving. I hope you do as well.
